entries.title: Resumption of CTA train service across Lake Street bridge delayed yet again
entries.summary: <p>Completion of work on the Lake Street bridge has been delayed once again, causing continued service disruptions on the CTA's Green and Pink lines.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.chicago.gov/content/dam/city/depts/cdot/bridge/LakeStreetBridge_VirtualPublicMeeting_Slides%20(09.24.25).pdf" target="_blank" >Improvements to the 110-year-old bascule bridge</a> include replacing its west leaf, its deck, substructures and CTA tracks, and rehabilitating the bridge’s houses and mechanical and electrical systems. It <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago/2025/09/28/lake-street-bridge-repairs-closure-chicago" >has been closed to vehicles and pedestrians</a> since about a year ago, but CTA trains had continued to traverse its upper level until earlier this month.</p><p>Train service was to be completed in time to allow CTA service on the Green and Pink lines <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/10/12/lake-street-bridge-cta-green-pink" >to resume early Monday</a>. That had been <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/10/25/lake-street-bridge-closure-cta-green-pink-lines-reroute" >delayed until 4 a.m. Wednesday</a>. It is now expected to reopen to trains "later this week."</p><p>The work is part of ongoing maintenance that began last fall with a similar closure. Even after train service resumes, the bridge will remain closed to vehicles and pedestrians until January 2028.</p><p></p><p>Until it reopens, Green Line trains will continue operating in two segments: from the Harlem/Lake stop at its western end to Clinton, and back; and from Clark/Lake in the Loop to its two South Side terminals. Shuttle buses will carry passengers between the Clinton and Clark/Lake stations. </p><p>Inbound Green Line trains from the South Side will travel clockwise around the Loop before heading south again.</p><p>Pink Line riders will still be able to ride all the way into the Loop over a more circuitous route; trains will operate between 54th/Cermak and the Racine Blue Line station, where passengers can transfer to the Blue Line into downtown. Pink Line trains will not operate in the Loop.<br></p><ul class="rte2-style-ul" type="disc" style="margin-bottom: 0in; color: rgb(34, 34, 34); font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif; font-size: small; font-style: normal; font-variant-ligatures: normal; font-variant-caps: normal; font-weight: 400; letter-spacing: normal; orphans: 2; text-align: start; text-indent: 0px; text-transform: none; widows: 2; word-spacing: 0px; -webkit-text-stroke-width: 0px; white-space: normal; background-color: rgb(255, 255, 255); text-decoration-thickness: initial; text-decoration-style: initial; text-decoration-color: initial; margin-top: 0in;" id="rte-9bdc9de0-d266-11f1-b26d-b76b199e89bc"></ul>

entries.title: Man fatally shot in head in Roseland
entries.summary: <p>A man was fatally shot in Roseland Tuesday evening, according to Chicago police.</p><p>The man, 59, was in the 10500 block of South Eggleston Avenue at 6:01 p.m. when he was shot in the head, police said. He was taken to Christ Medical Center in Oak Lawn where he later died.</p><p>No one is in custody. An investigation is ongoing, police said. </p>

entries.title: East Aurora District 131 board member facing federal charges over fraud, kickback scheme
entries.summary: <p>An East Aurora School District 131 board member and former board president is facing multiple federal charges for orchestrating a bribery and fraud scheme, according to court documents filed Tuesday.</p><p>Annette Johnson — then-president of the District 131 Board and current board member serving on the district's finance and personnel committee — faces wire fraud charges in connection with the alleged plot that occurred between August 2021 and May 2023, according to prosecutors. </p><p>A federal grand jury in November 2025 approved the charges. Johnson is set to remain on the board through April 2029, according to the district's website.</p><p>While employed at the district, Johnson was also simultaneously serving as the chief financial officer of a company and two other affiliated companies, none of which are named in the complaint.</p><p> </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> entries.title: Off-duty FBI agent fatally shot man who was firing into crowd in Pilsen, officials say
entries.summary: <p>An off-duty FBI agent shot and killed a man he saw firing into a crowd Monday evening in Pilsen, the agency said in a statement.</p><p>The agent was driving home from work in an FBI vehicle around 5:30 p.m. when he saw the man "discharging a firearm into a group of innocent people" near 18th Street and Union Avenue, according to the FBI. At least two shots were fired before the agent intervened "to stop the ongoing threat," the FBI said.</p><p>When Chicago cops rushed to an officer-in-distress call around the time of the shooting, they found the 41-year-old agent aiming at the gunman after he'd been wounded, according to a Chicago police report. A handgun was found under a bicycle, the report said.</p><p>The gunman, identified as 27-year-old Oscar Isaya-Corrales, had suffered gunshot wounds to both legs, his chest and right flank, according to the police report and the Cook County medical examiner's office. </p><p>Isaya-Corrales<b> </b>was later pronounced dead at Stroger Hospital, less than an hour after he was shot, authorities said. His death was ruled a homicide, according to the medical examiner's office.</p><p>The FBI said the agent wasn't injured. An agent with the same name listed on the police report joined the FBI in March 2017 and had also worked in Seattle, according to federal court records.</p><p>"The FBI takes all shooting incidents involving our agents or task force members seriously," the agency said in a statement. "In accordance with FBI policy, the shooting incident is under review by the FBI’s Inspection Division."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item"> <bsp-carousel Chris Ridgeway, a manager at Pacific Garden, said Isaya-Corrales lived in the shelter from January until March and later for a few weeks in May. entries.title: Wyatt Kaiser finding his stride after helping Blackhawks earn much-needed win
entries.summary: <p>Wyatt Kaiser's game-winning goal Tuesday for the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a> was actually a deja vu moment.</p><p>Kaiser slipped down the left side, received a pass from Frank Nazar in the slot and ripped a shot through Kings goalie Anton Forsberg's five-hole to give the Hawks a 2-1 lead with less than 13 minutes to play. They ultimately hung on for a much-needed victory.</p><p>The play was almost an exact replica of Kaiser's goal <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2025/12/05/blackhawks-kings-penalty-kill-ilya-mikheyev-wyatt-kaiser" >last December</a> in Los Angeles, which also ended up being the game-winning marker in a 2-1 Hawks win. That coincidence wasn't lost on either the scorer or the passer. </p><p>"I was laughing; Frank was laughing," Kaiser said, adding that five-hole has become his preferred shooting target in the NHL.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">GOAL: Wyatt Kaiser goes five-hole on a shot from the circle to give the Blackhawks the lead. <a href="https://t.co/k4RbeSp0Bj">pic.twitter.com/k4RbeSp0Bj</a></p>— BHF (@BlackhawksFocus) <a href="https://x.com/BlackhawksFocus/status/2115266627029913758?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">October 28, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>That goal last December sparked a quietly impressive stretch in which Kaiser scored five times in a six-week span — a veritable hot streak for a Hawks defenseman, considering how little they've contributed offensively as a group in recent seasons.</p><p>Kaiser will hope for another pattern repeat now. His game has quietly improved as this season has progressed, and he's at a point now where a hot streak — or at least a stretch of lock-down defensive play — seems possible.</p><p>When he's dialed in, his lateral quickness and agility allow him to close off and suffocate opposing forwards in a unique and (for them) frustrating way. </p><p>His gap control tends to make or break his game, and it made it Tuesday. He made a crucial play at the defensive blue line about two minutes after his goal, for example, to deny a potential Kings breakaway.</p><p>"Kaiser was excellent tonight," coach Jeff Blashill said. "His compete was unreal. He’s played a number of good games in a row now. </p><p>"[To] start the year, didn’t have his A-game by any stretch. I think he’s gotten back to being smart and efficient with the puck and competing. When he does that, he’s a really good player."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-8f0000" Photos</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3><b>Compete level</b></h3><p>For not only Kaiser but also the entire Hawks roster, the compete level Tuesday was the highest it has been all season. It was consistently high, too, outside of the first five minutes.</p><p>"We've talked a lot about the mentality of, 'Hey, the systems can be the systems. But if we’re not winning battles and out-competing the other team and wanting it more, it doesn’t really matter,'" Kaiser said. </p><p>"So we've been really trying to emphasize, 'Win your battles, compete, beat the other guys.' You saw a little bit of that tonight. Hopefully [we'll] continue to build off that."</p><p>Even Connor Bedard embodied that with an essentially game-clinching play with 20 seconds left. He aggressively blocked a shot to clear the defensive zone, then got to the puck first and drew a penalty.</p><p>"[Bedard] gets knocked about defense more than he should," Blashill said. "There’s a reason why he’s out there at the end of the game. Because when the game is on the line, he is hyper-competitive. He's a hyper-competitive player, man. I'll go to war with that kid anytime. And that block is indicative of that."</p><h3><b>Lineup shuffle</b></h3><p>Blashill dramatically shuffled the forward lines, which yielded one trio that particularly clicked: Nazar centering Oliver Moore and Patrick Kane. The Hawks outshot the Kings 10-1 with them on the ice.</p><p>Flipping Kane and Bedard to opposite sides of the power play ignited that unit, as well. They broke a long power-play drought with Roman Kantserov's tying goal late in the second period.</p>

entries.title: Two men shot overnight in Loop - one fatally
entries.summary: <p>Two men were shot, one fatally, early Wednesday in the Loop. </p><p>The two were found in the first block of East Lake Street around 2:40 a.m., Chicago police said. One man, whose age was unknown, was shot multiple times in the body and taken to Northwestern Memorial Hospital where he was pronounced dead. </p><p>The other man, 38, was shot in the right leg and also taken to Northwestern where he was in fair condition, officials said. </p><p>No arrests were reported by police. </p><p>Area 3 detectives were investigating.</p>

entries.title: Blackhawks' Oliver Moore sets example with response to benching: 'He's so self-accountable'
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a> coach Jeff Blashill has clearly worried less about letting expletives slip into his interviews lately. </p><p>His latest curse came Tuesday morning — before the Hawks' <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/10/27/blackhawks-wyatt-kaiser-kings-goals-gap-control" >2-1 win</a> over the Kings — when quoting actor Robert Downey Jr., who once described his response to feedback from directors as, "Listen, smile, agree, and then do whatever the [bleep] you were gonna do anyway."</p><p>"There’s reality in that," Blashill said, relating it to Hawks players. "They have to go out and...not think, 'What does Blash want me to do?' You have to play based on how you've been trained by us. That's kind of your instincts. Then we'll coach you when you come back."</p><p>The right balance of trusting instincts versus following directions is different for every player, too. Artyom Levshunov, for example, tends to play better when he's leaning toward the former and letting his instincts take over. </p><p>Oliver Moore is also searching for that balance.</p><p>"I know I have an identity that I want to play to. I've found that," Moore said Tuesday. "But it's just [about] reminding myself of that. That'll make hockey feel like a little bit less thinking and more just flowing and playing."</p><p>One bad habit the Hawks are still trying to coach out of Moore is his tendency to attempt passes in the offensive zone that would lead to dangerous scoring chances if they reached their target — but that have extremely low probability of actually reaching that target.</p><p>He tried one such so-called "hope play" last week during the first period against the Canadiens. In that case, it was a behind-the-back backhand pass into the slot, hoping to hit Ryan Greene. </p><p>But there were two Canadiens players in the way who easily intercepted the puck and ended the Hawks' offensive-zone cycle. The Canadiens ended up scoring later on that shift.</p><p>When Moore was healthy-scratched Sunday against the Panthers, that lowlight was a key part of the instructional video he watched.</p><p>"Your eyes get lit up if you see a play going into the slot...[and] I think I'm a player who can make plays," Moore said. "But I just have to find a better balance."</p><p>Blashill said he thought Moore had actually been playing well overall before Sunday, but he decided a message had to be sent — to Moore and the entire team — about not "beating themselves."</p><p>Moore returned to the Hawks' lineup Tuesday and found immediate chemistry on a new line with Frank Nazar and Patrick Kane. They dominated most of their shifts against the Kings, out-shooting them 10-1.</p><p>"[Moore and Nazar] can create so much with their speed," Kane said. "We had couple zone entries where we’re pushing their 'D' back, and it creates space for that next layer."</p><p>Said Blashill: "The credit I give to Oliver [is], every time I talk to anybody that's been around him, they always rave about him. Because he's that kind of person. He's so self-accountable, yet he's super comfortable in his own skin, too. He can shake [mistakes] off and go back it."</p><p>Moore was on the ice for Wyatt Kaiser's game-winning goal but didn't earn a point on it, leaving him stuck on two goals and one assist in 11 games this season.</p><p>Despite Moore's lack of box-score productivity, his speed always makes him noticeable. He has taken strides (pun intended) when it comes to learning how to utilize it effectively.</p><p>"I've done a better job getting into areas to use my speed, picking out holes," Moore said. "There's been examples of that. Off the rush, I've been better knowing when to make play and when not to. </p><p>"But just in the 'O'-zone, if I can continue to use my feet down there and make it hard on teams, that's the growth I want to see."</p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Husband cheated long ago; now her former flames keep resurfacing
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I am 39 and have been with my husband for 20 years. We got together when we were young, and our two kids are almost grown. Early in our relationship, he cheated on me several times. I was able to move past that for the most part. We have a solid relationship and life now. A few of my ex-boyfriends have reached out to me over the last 18 months. I have removed myself from all social media and job websites, but they keep finding me.</p><p>One of these men is occupying more time in my head than he should. I cannot stop thinking about him, and about a year ago we connected over the phone. Nothing happened in person. I felt awful, and I told him I could no longer talk to him. He found me again through a friend, and intruding thoughts are creeping back in all the time.</p><p>I never got the opportunity to date around like my spouse did; he has slept with many women. I have only ever slept with him. I feel like I missed out on something. I think I know the answer, but I can't talk to anyone else about this. — <i>WONDERING IN THE NORTHWEST</i></p><p><b>DEAR WONDERING:</b> Don't risk your solid relationship on a what-if. Your husband's decades-old indiscretions are not an excuse to cheat on him now. Instead of moving past them "for the most part," let them go completely. They are ancient history. Block the ex-boyfriend and ask your friends to stop giving out your number without your permission. If you need to rekindle the passion with your husband, consult a licensed couples counselor, either with him or on your own.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My wife and I have some longtime friends who said they would be passing through our area. We invited them to have dinner with us and spend the night during their trip. They readily accepted and confirmed their afternoon arrival date and time a week in advance.</p><p>Two hours before they were supposed to be here, we got a call from them saying, "Mix-up. We're busy tonight, so push dinner back to 10:30 p.m., and then we'll spend the entire next day visiting with you instead!" This was a huge imposition because we never eat dinner that late (bedtime for us is around 10), and we already had plans for the next day.</p><p>We adapted and offered them some light appetizers and dessert when they arrived at nearly 11 p.m. We then excused ourselves to retire at midnight after setting them up in the guest room. We reminded them we had to be on our way by 10 the next morning for an existing commitment, but that we could visit over coffee and pastries here beforehand. They said they prefer to sleep late (until almost noon) and seemed genuinely miffed that we didn't change our plans for them. How would you have handled this? — <i>MIXED UP IN ARIZONA</i></p><p><b>DEAR MIXED UP:</b> I would have handled the situation the same way you did, and in the future, I would not agree to host that presumptuous couple again. Ever.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i></p>
entries.author: Abigail Van Buren

entries.title: New Jersey's decades-old voter intimidation campaign is a cautionary tale as midterms near
entries.summary: <p>In the <a class="Link" href="https://ugapress.org/book/9780820357744/voter-suppression-in-u-s-elections/" target="_blank" >history of voter suppression</a> in the United States, including attempts to stop <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2020/04/11/opinion/sunday/republicans-voter-suppression.html" target="_blank" >Black</a> and <a class="Link" href="https://splinternews.com/the-forgotten-history-of-how-latinos-earned-the-right-t-1793862634" target="_blank" >Latino people</a> from voting, Republican tactics in the 1981 New Jersey gubernatorial race stand out.</p><p>That November, voters in several cities saw posters at polling places printed in bright red letters: “WARNING. This area is being patrolled by <a class="Link" href="https://www.wnyc.org/story/armed-men-once-patrolled-polls-will-they-reappear-november/" target="_blank" >the National Ballot Security Task Force</a>.”</p><p>About 200 patrols were deployed statewide, many of them uniformed and carrying guns.</p><p>In Trenton, patrol members asked a Black voter for her registration card and turned her away when she didn’t produce it. Latino voters were prevented from voting in Vineland, while in Newark some voters were physically chased from the polls by patrolmen, one of whom warned a poll worker not to stay at her post after dark. Similar scenes played out in at least two other cities, Camden and Atlantic City.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-090000" name="module-090000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Commentary bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Commentary</h2></div> </div><p>Weeks later, after a recount, Republican <a class="Link" href="https://njmonthly.com/articles/jersey-living/the-governor-at-80/" target="_blank" >Thomas Kean</a> won election as governor by fewer than 1,800 votes.</p><p>Democrats, however, soon won a significant victory. With local civil rights activists, they discovered that the “ballot security” operation was a joint project of the state and national Republican committees. They filed suit in December 1981, <a class="Link" href="https://www.brennancenter.org/sites/default/files/legacy/Democracy/dnc.v.rnc/1981%20complaint.pdf" target="_blank" >charging Republicans with “efforts to intimidate, threaten and coerce</a> duly qualified black and Hispanic voters.”</p><p>In November 1982, the case was settled when the <a class="Link" href="https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/court-cases/dnc-v-rnc-consent-decree" target="_blank" >Republican committees signed a federal consent decree</a> — a court order applicable to activities anywhere in the U.S. — agreeing not to use race in selecting targets for ballot security activities and to refrain from deploying armed poll watchers.</p><p>That decree <a class="Link" href="https://www.npr.org/2018/01/09/576858203/decades-old-consent-decree-lifted-against-rncs-ballot-security-measures" target="_blank" >expired in 2018</a> after Democrats failed to convince a judge to renew it.</p><p>The 1981 voter suppression efforts resonate today in the midst of the <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/14/us/politics/supreme-court-trump-mail-in-ballots.html" target="_blank" >Trump administration’s persistent efforts</a> to <a class="Link" href="https://www.reuters.com/world/us-supreme-court-lifts-judicial-hurdle-trumps-mail-in-ballot-curbs-2026-08-24/" target="_blank" >suppress the vote</a> and <a class="Link" href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/show/trump-tries-to-undermine-trust-in-elections-but-documents-dont-support-his-claims" target="_blank" >undermine trust in elections</a> nationwide.</p><p>In May, a PBS reporter asked President Donald Trump whether he would send the National Guard or U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents to polling places in the midterm elections.</p><p>“<a class="Link" href="https://x.com/ElizLanders/status/2054265101322993816?s=20" target="_blank" ><u>He did not rule it out</u></a>,” wrote reporter Liz Landers.</p><h3>Republican ‘ballot security’ plan</h3><p>Considered an early referendum on Ronald Reagan’s presidency, New Jersey’s 1981 gubernatorial race featured Kean — with <a class="Link" href="https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2008/06/02/the-dirty-trickster" target="_blank" >Roger Stone</a> at the campaign’s helm — promising corporate tax cuts and relying heavily on Reagan’s endorsement.</p><p>State and national Republican party officials then devised a project they claimed would prevent Democratic cheating at the polls.</p><p>In the summer of 1981, the Republican National Committee sent an operative named John A. Kelly to New Jersey to run a ballot security effort. Kelly had previously served as one of the <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/1981/11/13/nyregion/kelly-reported-on-reagan-s-appointees.html" target="_blank" >RNC’s liaisons to the Reagan White House</a>.</p><p>In August 1981, under the guise of the National Ballot Security Taskforce, Kelly sent about 200,000 letters marked “return to sender” to voters in heavily Black and Latino districts. Those whose letters were returned had their names added to a list of voters to be challenged at the polls on Election Day, a tactic known as <a class="Link" href="https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/guide-voter-caging" target="_blank" >voter caging</a>.</p><p>In the Newark area, Kelly produced a list of 20,000 voters whom he deemed potentially fraudulent. He then hired local operatives to organize patrols, ostensibly to keep such fraud at bay. To run the Newark operation, <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/1981/11/17/nyregion/imperiale-called-a-chief-in-gop-poll-security.html" target="_blank" >he hired Anthony Imperiale</a>.</p><h3><b>White vigilante</b></h3><p>Imperiale, in turn, hired off-duty police officers and employees of his private business, the Imperiale Security Police, to patrol voting sites in the city.</p><p>The gun-toting, barrel-chested former Marine had first adopted the security role during <a class="Link" href="https://njmonthly.com/articles/historic-jersey/the-rebellion-in-newark/" target="_blank" >Newark’s 1967 uprising</a> — five days of protests and a deadly occupation of the city by police and the National Guard following the police beating of a Black cab driver. During the uprising, Imperiale organized patrols of his predominantly white neighborhood .to keep “<a class="Link" href="https://nyti.ms/1Y8zykR" target="_blank" >the riots</a>” out.</p><p>Soon, Imperiale became was a hero of white backlash politics. His <a class="Link" href="http://riseupnewark.com/Flyer-North-Ward-Citizens-Committee/" target="_blank" >opposition to police reform</a> earned him widespread support from law enforcement. And his <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/1972/12/05/archives/kawaida-towers-confrontation-in-the-north-ward-of-newark.html" target="_blank" >fight against Black housing development</a> in Newark’s North Ward delighted many of his neighbors. By the end of the 1970s, Hollywood was <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/1979/10/30/archives/notes-on-people-argentine-exile-fearing-reprisals-cancels.html" target="_blank" >making a movie</a> based on his activities.</p><p>After serving as an independent in both houses of the state legislature, <a class="Link" href="https://newjerseyglobe.com/legislature/14103/" target="_blank" >Imperiale became a Republican in 1979</a>. Two years later, he campaigned with Kean.</p><p>Once in office, the new governor named Imperiale director of a new one-man state Office of Community Safety — an appointment often interpreted as reward for Imperiale’s leadership of the ballot efforts in Newark, but stymied when <a class="Link" href="https://nyti.ms/29KrnJG" target="_blank" >Democrats refused to fund the position</a>.</p><h3><b>Outcome and legacy</b></h3><p>Despite Kean’s slim margin of victory, Democrats at the time were careful not to claim that Republican voter suppression efforts had decided the election. In 2016, the former Democratic candidate claimed <a class="Link" href="https://www.wnyc.org/story/armed-men-once-patrolled-polls-will-they-reappear-november/" target="_blank" >they did indeed make the difference</a>.</p><p>Rather, the state and national Democratic committees brought suit against the RNC to ensure it couldn’t again use such methods anywhere. For nearly 40 years — through <a class="Link" href="https://www.brennancenter.org/sites/default/files/legacy/Democracy/dnc.v.rnc/1987%20consent%20decree.pdf" target="_blank" >amendments</a> and <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2009/12/03/us/politics/03voting.html" target="_blank" >challenges</a> — the resulting consent decree <a class="Link" href="https://talkingpointsmemo.com/edblog/this-should-keep-the-black-vote-down-considerably" target="_blank" >helped curtail</a> <a class="Link" href="https://www.democracynow.org/2008/9/18/lost_homes_lost_votes_are_republicans" target="_blank" >voter suppression tactics</a>.</p><p>After the decree’s expiration in 2018, Republicans ramped up their <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2020/05/18/us/Voting-republicans-trump.html" target="_blank" >recruitment of poll watchers</a> for the 2020 presidential election. After his loss in that election, Trump led a campaign aimed at <a class="Link" href="https://www.reuters.com/world/us/trump-claims-2020-election-rigged-least-107-times-six-months-midterms-loom-2026-05-26/" target="_blank" >discrediting the vote’s legitimacy, claiming fraud and irregularities</a> that he’s been <a class="Link" href="https://www.npr.org/2026/07/17/nx-s1-5896389/trump-revisits-debunked-theories-about-the-2020-election-in-primetime-speech" target="_blank" >consistently unable to prove</a>.</p><p>Since winning in 2024, Trump has led a comprehensive effort to <a class="Link" href="https://theconversation.com/why-the-supreme-court-blocked-trump-and-the-postal-service-from-restricting-mail-in-voting-for-the-midterms-291319" target="_blank" >discredit and suppress mail voting</a>. And the Department of Justice, Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon posted on X, has a “<a class="Link" href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/09/25/politics/trump-election-monitors-voting-machines-vis" target="_blank" >plan to send 1,000 federal election monitors</a> to select locations around the country to observe the midterm elections next week. This will be the largest monitoring effort in @theJusticeDept history!”</p><p>In addition to those efforts, CNN reports that “<a class="Link" href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/09/25/politics/trump-election-monitors-voting-machines-vis" target="_blank" >the Republican National Committee is training</a> new ‘special monitors’ to scrutinize voting machines.”</p><p>Next week, Republican tactics in 1981 are worth remembering. They demonstrate that the safeguarding of polling places from allegedly fraudulent voters and of public places from supposedly threatening people of color share not only a logic.</p><p>They also share a history.</p><p><i>Mark Krasovic is an associate professor of history and American studies at Rutgers University-Newark.</i></p><p><i>This </i><a class="Link" href="https://theconversation.com/armed-poll-watchers-new-jerseys-1981-racist-voter-intimidation-campaign-is-a-cautionary-tale-ahead-of-2026-midterms-293166" target="_blank" ><i>article</i></a><i> originally appeared on </i><a class="Link" href="http://theconversation.com/" target="_blank" ><i>theconversation.com</i></a></p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> </div><p></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-010000" name="module-010000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Greenlight task force, Home for Good bill, to ease lives of Illinois' formerly incarcerated
entries.summary: <p>Time served in prison should be just that: time served. Once men and women have completed their sentences, they’ve paid their debt to society, as the saying goes. But for too many people, their sentence stretches far beyond the amount of time set by a judge. Their record stands in the way of jobs, stable housing, education and opportunities for decades to come.</p><p>Barriers to successful reentry, or what we call permanent punishments, affect every person who has been touched by the system. Job applications ask people to disclose if they’ve ever been convicted of a felony. Landlords often reject renters with criminal backgrounds. State and federal benefits may even be denied. These permanent punishments of past incarceration include legal, economic and societal obstacles that make it difficult for people to rebuild their lives and chart a new course forward.</p><p>It doesn’t have to stay that way. To effectively break down these barriers and put an end to permanent punishments, the <a class="Link" href="endpp.org" target="_blank" >Illinois Coalition to End Permanent Punishments</a> is working diligently with various state and local officials, organizations, companies and individuals to bring awareness to the ongoing challenges facing those who have been previously incarcerated and spur change.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-fb0000" name="module-fb0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Commentary bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Commentary</h2></div> </div><p>Our group, made up of Illinoisans who have been directly impacted by the criminal justice system, met this month to reaffirm our platform and priorities with a focus on advancing safety, stability and prosperity for all.</p><p>After successfully helping the passage of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/02/17/formerly-incarcerated-celebrate-passage-of-illinois-clean-slate-act" >Clean Slate Act</a> into law, automating the sealing of eligible records, the Illinois Coalition to End Permanent Punishments is now working to ensure that this law is being implemented properly and funded accordingly. Clean Slate, once funded, will standardize and streamline the process of sealing records eligible for expungement, opening doors that were previously closed to the formerly incarcerated population.</p><p>Building on that success, we are pushing legislation to create a Permanent Punishment Review Task Force. This task force will study Illinois’ permanent punishment laws, identify factors for modifying or eliminating them, evaluate models for periodic review and recommend changes to the General Assembly. The House passed legislation that allows the creation of the task force — <a class="Link" href="https://www.ilga.gov/Legislation/BillStatus?DocTypeID=HB&DocNum=5091&GAID=18&SessionID=114&LegID=166635" target="_blank" >House Bill 5091</a> — in the spring. Now, we need to get it across the finish line when the Senate returns for veto session in November.</p><p>The Illinois Coalition to End Permanent Punishments is also working to pass the<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/03/19/home-for-good-event-promotes-second-chances-for-ex-prisoners" > Home for Good legislation</a> through the Senate. This legislation aims to create a comprehensive statewide strategy to improve housing and support services for people returning from prison. Access to affordable housing is another key component to ensuring a smooth reentry back into society. Not only is stable housing vital to help ensure people can meet the conditions of their release, it also provides the security needed to maintain a job, pursue education and address physical and mental health issues. We also know that increasing access to housing reduces recidivism, which helps advance public safety while also saving taxpayers money.</p><p>The benefits of these efforts reach far beyond the individual. When we remove barriers that prevent people from truly being able to live freely, we can build stronger communities that benefit everyone.</p><p>Those who have been impacted by permanent punishments will continue to share their stories and push for change. We urge policymakers across Illinois to listen and act on the experiences of your constituents to ensure that they are able to break free of the systems that are holding them back and contribute to a stronger Illinois for all.</p><p><i>Marlon Chamberlain is the founding executive director of the Illinois Coalition to End Permanent Punishments.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-e20000" name="module-e20000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Maternity ward closures in Illinois hospitals are part of national crisis
entries.summary: <p>After 40 years of practicing obstetrics in Chicago, I never imagined that one of the greatest threats to maternal and newborn safety would not be a medical complication, but the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/09/02/prime-healthcare-cuts-obstetrics-care-at-3-chicago-area-hospitals" >closure of hospital maternity</a> units that have served generations of families.</p><p>I have witnessed extraordinary advances in medicine and cared for thousands of mothers and babies. Yet as medical science makes childbirth increasingly safer, we are witnessing a troubling reversal: Hospitals are eliminating maternity services, often redirecting resources toward more profitable areas of care. The hospitals remain open, but their delivery rooms close.</p><p>This is not an isolated phenomenon. It is a growing crisis.</p><p>Between 2016 and 2023, Illinois<a class="Link" href="https://www.cdc.gov/pcd/issues/2024/24_0332.htm" target="_blank" > lost 32 obstetric hospitals</a>, a 27% net reduction in birthing facilities. For pregnant women, closures mean longer travel, disrupted relationships with physicians, unfamiliar hospitals and potentially dangerous delays in emergencies. Communities also lose experienced teams whose expertise and trust took decades to build.</p><p>The financial pressures are real. Declining birth rates, inadequate reimbursement, rising operating costs and workforce shortages make maternity services difficult to sustain. But childbirth cannot be managed like an elective service. Hemorrhages, placental abruption and fetal distress do not wait for convenient hours. Safe obstetric care requires experienced professionals, operating rooms, anesthesia, blood banks and neonatal support around the clock.</p><p>If maternity care is essential, reimbursement must reflect the true cost of maintaining that readiness. We must also address the extraordinary medical liability pressures affecting obstetrics.</p><p>Illinois urgently needs uniform, enforceable standards before hospitals suspend or close maternity services. These must include assessments of patient travel times, emergency transportation, insurance coverage and the capacity of receiving hospitals to provide safe care.</p><p>Not every maternity unit can remain open indefinitely. But closure must be the last resort, not simply a financial decision made without adequate safeguards for patients and communities.</p><p>At a time when America is concerned about declining birth rates and an aging population, we should be making it easier — not harder — for families to have children safely.</p><p>Preserving maternity care is not simply about keeping delivery rooms open. It is about protecting mothers, babies and the future of our communities.</p><p><i>Dr. Maria Munoz,</i> <i>Morton Grove</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-240000" name="module-240000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Celebrating immigrants, country’s diversity</h3><p>Sometimes just a nudge can have seniors reminiscing and marveling how much they've been exposed to over the years, including the many wonderful immigrants they've met.</p><p>Lithuania supplied all four of my grandparents. Three came to Chicago via the iconic Ellis Island in its pre-World War I heyday. In my own slowly widening world, my childhood neighborhood had many German-and- Polish-born parents and grandparents, all earnest and industrious. Grade school introduced me to a mannerly Austrian kid who'd grow up to become an accomplished professional soccer goalie. Summer camp in Wisconsin delivered a native Irish counselor.</p><p>High school added Russians and Ukrainians to bolster our first soccer team. In college, I encountered students from Greece, India, Mexico, Nigeria and the Philippines. By late middle-age I spanned the alphabet, from Afghanistan to Zaire/the Congo. And in retirement, I keep filling openings, meeting former residents of Bosnia, Colombia, Ecuador, Jamaica and Tanzania.</p><p>Many U.S.-born adults share this experience. Hopefully, they also share my general satisfaction and question the idler tag often applied today to undocumented newcomers. Because from what I've seen, all are typically respectable and responsible people, practical, unspoiled, optimistic and resourceful enough to overcome assimilation's challenges.</p><p>That conviction prompts me to again endorse <a class="Link" href="https://win-brg.wa.gov/events/2024-10/national-immigrants-day-october-28" target="_blank" >National Immigrants Day</a> today — Oct. 28. President Ronald Reagan, who established the day back in 1987, grasped immigrants' cumulative contributions to the country through the decades.</p><p><i>Tom Gregg, Niles</i></p><h3><b>Voting is an act of justice, hope for marginalized communities </b></h3><p>Over three years ago <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2025/05/02/czuba-sentence-wadee-al-fayoumi" >Wadee AlFayoumi</a>, a 6-year-old Palestinian American Muslim boy, was murdered in a Chicago suburb. In those three years, our Palestinian, Muslim, Black, Brown and immigrant communities have continued facing an assault on our rights and identities — and we’ve organized together to demand better.</p><p>Protests. Legislative advocacy. "Know your rights" education. Rapid response networks. Coalition building and resource sharing.</p><p>We also have another tool — our vote.</p><p>Regardless of your background or political party, one thing is becoming harder for all to ignore: Our democracy is at a tipping point. The midterm elections are crucial to determine what comes next for our country.</p><p>Our tax dollars are funding <a class="Link" href="https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/un-inquiry-says-israel-kept-committing-genocide-gaza-after-truce-2026-10-26/" target="_blank" >Israel’s genocide</a>, forever wars and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement kidnappings instead of mental health support, basic needs and effective safety solutions. Attacks on voting rights and a surge in racism and anti-Muslim hate are concerted attempts to intimidate our communities out of the democratic process.</p><p>But despite the crises we’re facing, I hold onto hope.</p><p>In my role as executive director of the <a class="Link" href="https://muslimciviccoalition.org/" target="_blank" >Muslim Civic Coalition</a> — a nonpartisan community advocacy organization fighting for civic justice across Illinois — I hear from community members every day about their concerns and dreams for the future.</p><p>Many talk about the need to invest in our schools rather than foreign militaries, <a class="Link" href="https://news.gallup.com/poll/692948/u.s.-back-israel-military-action-gaza-new-low.aspx" target="_blank" >mirroring the polls</a> and what others from outside the community often tell me. </p><p>Even as free speech is stifled, we have built bridges, shifted opinions and educated policymakers, although much work remains. We know the power we hold, how to hold our public officials accountable and the difference we can make this November.</p><p>Like other traditions, our faith calls us to be engaged citizens, to support the oppressed and uphold justice. And when we all vote, we elect just leaders, protect our communities and create the future we deserve.</p><p>Key election information and how to report problems on Election Day are available in multiple languages at the coalition’s <a class="Link" href="https://muslimciviccoalition.org/voterhub" target="_blank" >online voter hub</a>.</p><p>Check it out. </p><p><i>Amina Barhumi, Orland Park</i><br></p>

entries.title: Chicago ditched school ratings years ago, but 1 in 5 school board candidates want to bring them back
entries.summary: <p>Jessica Biggs found a dream school for her artistic daughter where she gets drama and visual arts classes and is in an after-school dance troupe.</p><p>It’s a fine and performing arts magnet school far from her home on the South Side.</p><p>“She is incredibly talented, and as she was moving into middle school, we wanted to make sure that she was in a place that had programming that would be affirming to her, where she could really explore her creative self,” Biggs said at <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/10/14/4-takeaways-from-cps-school-board-president-forum" target="_blank" ><u>our recent forum for candidates</u></a> running to be president of the Chicago Board of Education.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/candidates/jessica-biggs/" target="_blank" ><u>Biggs</u></a> and her two opponents, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/candidates/hilario-dominguez/" target="_blank" ><u>Hilario Dominguez</u></a> and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/candidates/victor-p-henderson/" target="_blank" ><u>Victor Henderson</u></a>, say they want Chicago Public Schools to stay a district that offers a range of choices — including neighborhood, magnet, selective-enrollment and charter schools. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/school-board/president/" target="_blank" ><u>But the candidates differ</u></a> on how parents should go about choosing a school and how CPS should measure school quality.</p><p>The school board race has been <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2026/10/23/school-board-campaign-mailer-ads-fact-check/" target="_blank" ><u>dominated by political jabs</u></a> and the <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/chicago-school-board/2026/10/13/long-a-foregone-conclusion-property-tax-hikes-will-no-longer-be-a-given-under-elected-cps-board" target="_blank" ><u>district’s financial woes</u></a>, especially in the citywide president’s contest. But school choice is an issue that is important to parents and that the school board can change.</p><h3><b>Should CPS bring back ratings? </b></h3><p>Three years ago, the school board decided to <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2023/04/26/chicago-drops-public-school-ratings-in-favor-of-a-less-punitive-system-for-assessing-school" target="_blank" ><u>stop giving schools a singular rating</u></a>. In the past, CPS gave the lowest-performing schools a “Level 3” while the highest-performing got a “Level 1+.”</p><p>Those ratings gave parents an easy way to judge schools as they made decisions about where to send their children. CPS also used these ratings for accountability purposes.</p><p>Now CPS parents can check 20 different measures on a <a class="Link" href="https://www.cps.edu/schools/profiles/" target="_blank" ><u>school’s profile page</u></a>, including proficiency on standardized tests, staffing levels and whether the school has adopted a high-quality curriculum.</p><p>Ten of the 44 candidates running for school board want to see the ratings return. That includes Henderson, a prominent attorney running for board president.</p><p>“Ratings, in and of themselves, are not bad,” he said at the recent forum. “It’s feedback, and we can’t be afraid of feedback. We can't put our heads in the sand and be afraid to rate a school, a principal, a student, or even an Uber driver.”</p><p>Isaiah White, who is <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/school-board/districts/6a/" target="_blank" ><u>running to represent District 6a</u></a>, which covers some of the Near North Side and Downtown, said parents need an “exhaustive, reliable, and easily parsable information on school quality.”</p><p>“Selecting an institution for your student is a monumental decision; CPS should do all it can to support parents in making an informed choice,” he wrote on our candidate questionnaire.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>School board president candidates Jessica Biggs, Hilario Dominguez and Victor Henderson answered questions about how they chose or would choose schools for their children during an October candidate forum hosted by WBEZ, the Chicago Sun-Times and Chalkbeat.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times file</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>But most candidates, including Biggs and Dominguez, say giving a school a singular grade is too simplistic and doesn’t give parents a full view of all that’s going on. Biggs said the old CPS ratings, which were based on things like test scores and attendance, were more reflective of the resources CPS put into schools, rather than the education teachers and others provided.</p><p>“They're really set up to pick winners and losers, and I don't think that's the responsibility of the district,” she said.</p><p>Ratings also became a self-fulfilling prophecy. Schools with low ratings often had a hard time attracting students and were left mostly with students who were struggling.</p><p>Dominguez said ratings disproportionately hurt schools serving low-income Black and Latino students. He likened them to standardized tests, noting that <a class="Link" href="https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/social-sciences-and-humanities/test-bias/" target="_blank" ><u>how questions are framed and words are defined</u></a> can mean different things to different communities, which can show up in students’ scores.</p><p>He would like to see CPS move away from a system in which there are good and bad schools and everyone is competing to get into the coveted ones.</p><p>“We can't keep playing ‘The Hunger Games’ to find a quality school,” he said. “Every family deserves a quality option in their neighborhood, and that's what I'm going to fight for.”</p><h3><b>Should CPS continue to be a choice system?</b></h3><p>While Dominguez sees problems with the current system, he supports having options and concedes that, when his 1-year-old son goes to school, he will likely look at selective schools in addition to neighborhood options. Dominguez, the only board president candidate who went to CPS schools, attended a magnet elementary school and a selective-enrollment high school.</p><p>Most candidates agree with Dominguez that CPS shouldn’t eliminate school choice.</p><p>Only two school board candidates — Connie Anderson in the Southeast Side <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/school-board/districts/10b/" target="_blank" ><u>District 10b race</u></a> and Emma Lozano in the Southwest Side <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/school-board/districts/7a/" target="_blank" ><u>District 7a race</u></a> — said they wanted CPS to retreat from its choice system.</p><p>“While families value different programs, CPS should invest in every school so all students have access to strong academics, arts, enrichment, and support services close to home,” Lozano wrote on our questionnaire. “Every student deserves an excellent neighborhood school without relying on a complex choice system.”</p><p>While most candidates support some school choice, there’s varying views on privately managed charter schools, which have become an <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/06/10/chicago-charter-schools-cps-board-renewals-oversight-chicago-public-schools" target="_blank" ><u>increasingly controversial part of CPS’ portfolio</u></a>. Two decades ago, CPS was opening charter schools every year and parents flocked to them. They had lotteries and waiting lists.</p><p>But the powerful Chicago Teachers Union opposes using private operators to run public schools and has fought against charters. At the same time, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/09/24/chicago-public-schools-enrollment-drops-by-more-than-11-000-accelerating-long-term-downward-trend" target="_blank" ><u>school district is losing enrollment</u></a>, making it hard to justify opening schools. The last time CPS opened a new charter school was in 2019.</p><p>Groups that support charter schools and school choice <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/10/16/cash-floods-cps-school-board-races-with-big-money-groups-outraising-the-chicago-teachers-union-5-to-1" target="_blank" ><u>have been major donors in this school board election</u></a>.The political arm of the Illinois Network of Charter Schools has spent more than $2.3 million to support 19 candidates plus more than $600,000 to oppose Dominguez and Karen Zaccor, a retired teacher who opposes opening more charters and is running to represent District 4a on the North Side.</p><p>The group has not endorsed or spent any money supporting Henderson, a board member of the charter operator Urban Prep Academies. Henderson is the only candidate for board president who strongly supports charters and has indicated he is open to adding some. Illinois Network of Charter Schools officials did not respond to questions about why they have not endorsed anyone in the presidential race.</p><p>Most school board candidates — 27 of 44 — say they think the district should support charter schools that <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2025/11/19/chicago-public-schools-aspira-charter-network-finances-cps-investigation" target="_blank" ><u>get into financial trouble</u></a>, but just nine think that CPS should open more.</p>

entries.title: 'Charismatic' rare black fox that prowled Northbrook, intriguing and befuddling residents, is found dead
entries.summary: <p>A rare black-colored red fox that's been spotted in Northbrook for at least a year or two was recently found dead, according to wildlife officials who are awaiting test results to get a better picture of why it died.</p><p>Before its demise, the creature suffered some sort of physical trauma along the lines of getting hit by a car, said Cook County Forest Preserves wildlife biologist Chris Anchor.</p><p>But it also exhibited signs of other underlying health issues, he said, adding that more tests are being completed.</p><p>“Very sad,” Anchor said. “It’s a very charismatic animal, a beautiful animal.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-d80000" Nelson</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Gina Manski, the north suburb's animal control officer, said she got a call Oct. 9 of a dead black fox or coyote in a yard. Before even seeing it, she knew it was a fox, as it was a relatively well-known occupant of the community that had intrigued and puzzled residents for some time.</p><p>"I was very, very, very sad, I can tell you that," Manski said about the fox's death. "There were a lot of people who were sad. Hopefully he mated and passed that gene on."</p><p>The animal is believed to be the same fox written about in August by the Chicago Sun-Times, which noted the coloration is the result of a rare genetic quirk. Foxes like this are called “melanistic” because they have elevated levels of melanin that determines pigmentation.</p><p>Most red foxes are — given the name of the breed — reddish in color, skewing orange.</p><p>Preliminary tests found the fox had signs of a parasitic infection and an enlarged heart, among other problems. Anchor said studying why some wild creatures die is important so experts can detect trends in disease that can impact wildlife and, sometimes, humans.</p><p>While some people are alarmed upon seeing a fox, Manski said they're usually not bothersome to humans and "provide a service by eating a lot of rodents, especially mice."</p><p>While they're certainly not immune from vehicle strikes, a 2007 British study suggested red foxes in an urban environment overseas "appeared to reduce the mortality risk of minor category roads by changing ... activity patterns."</p><p>There have been other black foxes in the Chicago region. A black-colored red fox kit was spotted in far southwest suburban Lockport in 2024.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/parks-nature/2026/08/24/red-fox-melanistic-northbrook-wildlife-rare-chicago-coyotes" target="_blank" >Rare black fox, whose coloration is the result of a genetic quirk, makes home in Northbrook</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/suburban-chicago/2024/09/10/coyote-roaming-park-ridge-edison-park-mange-wildlife-chicago" target="_blank" >That’s not a chupacabra in Park Ridge, but a coyote with mange</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: We received more than 50 submissions of Chicago’s best Halloween displays. And the winner is…
entries.summary: <p>We asked for your Halloween displays and you delivered with your formidable, terrifying and inspiring cemeteries, graveyards and even a “frightalian” beef shop.</p><p>More than 50 bone-chilling photos and videos were submitted, demonstrating the limitless creativity of our neighbors. It was difficult to narrow it down to our favorites because there were so many fantastical and frightening displays, so thanks to all who entered. But three displays in particular caught our eye with Chicago-ness, attention to detail and sheer engineering. Read on to find out what they were and to hear from the architects themselves.</p><p>Make sure to check out all of the displays below and if you’re in the neighborhood, stop by and check them out on Halloween. The high will be in the low 60s with a chance of showers — but the threat of inclement weather will just add to the ambience.</p><h3>‘Jaw-knee’s Beef’ in Galewood</h3><p><i>Submitted by: Susie Jendro</i></p><p>HEEEEEEERE’S JAW-KNEE’S! Happy spooky season! My husband Mike and I are pleased to share our new Halloween display, themed after the one and only Johnnie's Beef in Elmwood Park. Johnnie’s is just down the street from us and we are big fans. What better way to celebrate the season and one of Chicago’s finest dining establishments than to turn our yard into a haunted homage?</p><p>This idea came to us shortly after Halloween 2025 when we decided we wanted to show up in a huge way for our neighborhood. I truly believe Galewood loves Halloween more than any Chicago neighborhood. When the Mars Factory recently left the area, we knew we had to go big. Mars was a huge boon to our hood’s Halloween spirit, generously handing out tons of candy, which brought hundreds, if not thousands, of festive trick-or-treaters to our street. We want to welcome every one of those families back to continue their Halloween traditions in Galewood!</p><p>We’re just doing what we can to keep the haunt alive (or…dead??). All ghouls big and small, young and old, spooky or sparkly are welcome to Galewood on Halloween where the candy is boontiful and the frightalian beefs are the best in the world!</p><p>Thanks to everyone who has stopped by to snap a pic or shared a post with us! It has really meant a lot for us to see people getting so much joy out of what we’ve made. Happy Halloween!</p><p><i>Come back later this week to hear more from Susie and Mike about their display.</i></p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> FBI agent fatally shot man firing into crowd: officials</a></h3><p></p><h5>Reporting by <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-yddldikd-l-k/" target="_blank" >Mohammad Samra</a> and <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-yddldikd-l-u/" target="_blank" >Sophie Sherry</a></h5><p><b>Fatal shooting</b>: An off-duty FBI agent fatally shot 27-year-old Oscar Isaya-Corrales Monday evening in Pilsen. According to the FBI, the agent was driving home from work in an FBI vehicle around 5:30 p.m. when he saw the man fire a gun "into a group of innocent people" near 18th Street and Union Avenue. The agent shot Isaya-Corrales "to stop the ongoing threat," the FBI said.</p><p><b>Records show</b>: When Chicago cops rushed to the scene, they found the FBI agent still aiming at Isaya-Corrales after he'd been wounded, according to a police report. A handgun was found under a bicycle, the report said. Isaya-Corrales suffered multiple gunshot wounds and was pronounced dead at Stroger Hospital. His death was ruled a homicide, records show.</p><p><b>Key context</b>: The feds described Isaya-Corrales as a Venezuelan national without legal status who had been "taken into custody at the border and subsequently released" in 2023. He had lived this year at the Pacific Garden Mission shelter on the Near West Side — a worker there told the Sun-Times that Isaya-Corrales did not have any family in the area. He came to the shelter to "try and make his life better," but struggled with drug addiction, the worker said.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-yddldikd-l-o/" Michael Sacks</a></h3><h3></h3><h5>Reporting by <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-yddldikd-l-p/" target="_blank" >Fran Spielman</a></h5><p><b>Billionaire boogeyman</b>: Mayor Brandon Johnson on Tuesday accused <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-yddldikd-l-x/" target="_blank" >billionaire businessman Michael Sacks</a> of leading a "nasty coalition of billionaires" who are using their wealth to elect school board members who would close more Chicago Public Schools.</p><p><b>Key context</b>: Johnson never mentioned Sacks by name. But it was clear who he was talking about, as Sacks has helped bankroll a political action committee known as Common Ground Collective that has raised more than $5 million to elect <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-yddldikd-l-m/" target="_blank" >Jessica Biggs</a> as school board president and other school board members who would not be beholden to the Chicago Teachers Union.</p><p><b>About the election</b>: For the first time, Chicagoans will elect the entire Board of Education — 20 members plus an at-large president. <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-yddldikd-l-c/" target="_blank" >Our free voter guide</a> helps you find your district and gives you the rundown on your candidates.</p><p><b>Meanwhile, at City Hall</b>: Three City Council leaders who negotiated the compromise that sweetened Stonepeak Partners' deal to acquire Chicago's parking meters are <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-yddldikd-l-q/" target="_blank" >calling a special City Council meeting Monday</a>. Then in mid-October, temperatures hit 88 degrees in Chicago. With all that considered, experts say Chicago can expect a milder winter.</p><p><b>Winter outlook</b>: That's thanks to the potential of a "historically strong" El Niño, according to the National Weather Service's winter outlook report. That means a 50% to 60% chance of above-normal temperatures this winter. entries.title: Cubs’ Pete Crow-Armstrong voted Player of the Year in Players Choice Awards as award-season haul begins
entries.summary: <p>Pete Crow-Armstrong didn’t need to wait till now to start clearing space on his mantle.</p><p>But as baseball's award season gets underway in the wake of Crow-Armstrong’s spectacular campaign, the hardware is starting to roll in.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" target="_blank" >Cubs</a>’ center fielder was named Player of the Year and National League Outstanding Player when the players’ union announced the winners of its Players Choice Awards on Wednesday.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Written in the stars: a PCA for PCA. 🤩 Congratulations to Pete Crow-Armstrong on being voted the Player of the Year in the 2026 Players Choice Awards!<a href="https://x.com/Cubs?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">@Cubs</a> <a href="https://t.co/YMS3zyRhSO">pic.twitter.com/YMS3zyRhSO</a></p>— MLBPA (@MLBPA) <a href="https://x.com/MLBPA/status/2115413506136924254?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">October 28, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>As the title indicates, the Players Choice Awards were voted on by Crow-Armstrong’s peers, a notable difference from other end-of-season awards.</p><p>Crow-Armstrong is expected to be announced as an award-winner plenty more this offseason. He was among the finalists for the Hank Aaron Award, given to each league’s best hitter, and a finalist for a Gold Glove. It is anticipated he’ll win the NL MVP.</p><p>But despite being well deserving of those honors – Crow-Armstrong led baseball with 10.8 fWAR, ranked first in the game in home runs (45) and runs scored (119), tied for third in stolen bases (41) and was fourth in RBIs (107) – he spent the season expressing little excitement over his many individual accomplishments as he posted the seventh 40-40 campaign ever and rewrote much of the franchise record book.</p><p>Instead, Crow-Armstrong kept his focus on team goals, and he was obviously a massive part of the Cubs reaching the postseason for the second straight year. But he also acknowledged his no-show in the team’s brief, disappointing two-game stay in the playoffs, going 0-for-7 with four strikeouts as the Cubs were swept out of the wild-card round by the Padres.</p><p>That, however, will not tarnish what was a remarkable, all-timer of a regular season that will earn him a lot more than just a couple Players Choice Awards by the time baseball’s awards season is over and done with.</p>

entries.title: Dolores Huerta, influential labor leader, feminist and civil rights icon, dies at 96
entries.summary: <p>Dolores Huerta, who co-founded the United Farm Workers union to improve working conditions in the nation’s fruit and vegetable fields and coined the phrase “Sí, se puede!” that became a widespread rallying cry, has died. She was 96.</p><p>Huerta’s family said she died Wednesday at home.</p><p>“We know that many of you around the world share in our mourning, and we will be following up on plans to recognize and celebrate her incredible life and legacy,” they said in a statement shared by her foundation.</p><p>Huerta kept a busy schedule well into her 90s, marching in protests and speaking across the country about race, poverty, LGBTQ+ and women’s rights on behalf of her Bakersfield, California-based foundation.</p><p>Huerta’s resolve cemented her place in history as one of the nation’s most influential labor leaders, civil rights icons and feminist activists. Her three-word Spanish-language slogan — which translates to “Yes, it can be done” — was grounded in the belief that people who take action can affect change.</p><p>Her work over the decades earned her accolades including the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the nation’s highest civilian honor. When President Barack Obama presented the award in 2012, he praised Huerta as a tenacious leader and noted that he had stolen her slogan for his 2008 campaign.</p><p>This year, Huerta sent shock waves through the Latino community when she revealed that she was sexually abused in the 1960s by the farmworker movement’s co-founder, César Chavez, leading to the birth of two children, a secret she had kept for 60 years, long after he died.</p><p>From the early 1970s on, Huerta’s life partner was Richard Chavez, César’s brother, and together they had four kids. She also had seven children from two earlier marriages.</p><p>Huerta said she had kept silent for so long because she feared coming forward would compromise her life’s work and unravel all the progress made for workers.</p><p>When asked during a 2026 interview with the news organization Latino USA about keeping the secret, Huerta said: “It was my personal pain, it was my personal problem and, you know, I think it was worth it because it was my cross to bear. I’ll say it that way.”</p><h4>Homegrown activism</h4><p>Huerta was born Dolores Clara Fernandez in 1930 in Dawson, New Mexico. Her father was a miner and union activist who won a seat in the state Legislature. Her parents divorced when she was 3, and her mother took her and her brothers to California.</p><p>Immersed in a melting pot of Mexican, Filipino, African American, Japanese and Chinese working families, Huerta learned from her mother — who owned a restaurant and hotel — about independence, compassion and activism.</p><p>Huerta was a young, energetic elementary school teacher in the agricultural San Joaquin Valley when she decided to answer another calling after growing frustrated by her students’ poor living conditions.</p><p>“I couldn’t stand seeing kids come to class hungry and needing shoes,” she said in a 2017 PBS Independent Lens documentary on her life. “I thought I could do more by organizing farmworkers than by trying to teach their hungry children.”</p><p>Huerta’s early work with a civil rights group in Stockton resulted in her meeting Chavez. The two wanted to focus more on the plight of farmworkers, so in 1962 they started the National Farm Workers Association, which became United Farm Workers of America a few years later. She was a key leader and negotiator for the union for years.</p><p>She was among those who joined Filipino grape pickers on the picket line in what became the five-year “Delano Grape Strike.” With Chavez, she negotiated collective bargaining agreements and contracts with big growers, winning the first health and benefit plans for farmworkers.</p><p>Chavez, who died in 1993, once described her as fearless, committed to the cause and tough when it came to negotiations.</p><h4>On the campaign trail</h4><p>She met Sen. Robert Kennedy of Massachusetts during his visit to Delano in 1968 and volunteered with his presidential campaign, registering Mexican Americans in California to vote. Huerta was on stage with Kennedy after he won the California primary and he publicly thanked her, moments before he was shot.</p><p>The assassination devastated Huerta, but she kept organizing. Huerta was jailed 22 times for union demonstrating.</p><p>In 1988, she was seriously injured while protesting Republican presidential candidate George H.W. Bush’s opposition to the UFW grape boycott during his visit to San Francisco.</p><p>Caught in a crowd, she was struck by a police officer’s baton, suffered three broken ribs and a pulverized spleen, and required more than a dozen blood transfusions. She reached a settlement with the city to resolve her claims.</p><p>After a long recovery, Huerta shifted focus and hit the road to campaign for women’s rights and encourage Latinas to run for office.</p><p>She also campaigned for Democratic Presidents Bill Clinton, Obama and Joe Biden. California Gov. Gavin Newsom considered her a close friend.</p><h4>Fueled by courage</h4><p>Emilio Huerta, one of Dolores’ 13 children, said during an interview that his mother’s courage drove her life’s work.</p><p>“To dedicate your life to building a dream of a union for farmworkers, to take on agriculture, which to this day is still a powerhouse. ... That took a lot of guts,” he said.</p><p>Huerta learned the art of lobbying politicians, securing financial aid for the unemployed and disability insurance for California farmworkers. She spoke out against toxic pesticides, pushed for amnesty for immigrants in the country illegally and campaigned against federal guest worker programs.</p><p>By directing nationwide boycotts of grapes and lettuce in the early 1970s, she helped to create the economic pressure and political climate necessary for California to pass the first state law recognizing farmworkers’ right to collective bargaining.</p><p>Among her many accolades, she was the first Latina inducted into the National Women’s Hall of Fame, and she received nine honorary doctorates from U.S. universities. Schools are named in her honor in California, Texas and Colorado. Her image graces many murals, and streets bear her name.</p><p>But she didn’t always win favor with more liberal activists.</p><p>In 2016 when she endorsed Hillary Rodham Clinton instead of Sen. Bernie Sanders in the presidential Democratic primary, actor Rosario Dawson — a Sanders supporter who played Huerta in a 2014 movie about César Chavez — said Huerta had become “an instrument of the establishment.”</p><p>Dawson and Huerta eventually reconciled.</p><p>Guitarist Carlos Santana later oversaw a documentary based on Huerta’s life after the pair had a late-night conversation about music while in Hawaii. Santana, a Miles Davis fan, discovered Huerta was a huge fan of bebop legend Charlie Parker.</p><p>“I even met Charlie Parker. That’s my claim to fame,” Huerta joked during an interview with The Associated Press when she was 87.</p><p>Huerta’s work as a labor movement leader reverberated through the U.S. and beyond, making her name synonymous with civil rights. In the 2025 documentary “Seeds of Change: The Life and Legacy of Dolores Huerta,” she recounted her decades-long activism, and said the inspiration she drew from the women’s movement during the 1970s provided the validation she needed to take the stage with other labor leaders.</p><p>“I hope that my legacy will be one of an organizer that organized to fight injustice,” she said in the film. “We want to give our children an inheritance of justice, right, not jewels or property or money because they’ll just fight over it. So the main thing to do is to give them this love for justice — and that is the greatest gift I think that any of us can have.”</p>

entries.title: FBI agent involved in deadly shooting in Dixmoor
entries.summary: <p>A person was killed Wednesday morning in a shooting involving an FBI agent in south suburban Dixmoor, the agency said.</p><p>The shooting happened around 7 a.m. during "court-authorized law enforcement activity,'' the FBI said in a statement. The statement didn't include the address of the incident or note whether anyone was taken into custody. </p><p>Late Wednesday morning, residents looked on as Cook County sheriff's deputies and FBI agents blocked off the intersection of 145th Street and Cooper Avenue with vehicles and crime scene tape. There were at least 10 law enforcement officers at the scene, a residential area, as of 11 a.m. </p><p>"The FBI takes all shooting incidents involving our agents or task force members seriously," the agency said. "In accordance with FBI policy, the shooting incident is under review by the FBI’s Inspection Division. As this is an ongoing matter, we have no further details to provide."</p><p>On Monday evening, an off-duty FBI agent <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/27/fbi-agent-fatally-shoots-man-27-in-pilsen-chicago-police" >fatally shot a man</a> who was firing into a crowd in Chicago's Pilsen neighborhood, the FBI said. </p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/27/fbi-agent-fatally-shoots-man-27-in-pilsen-chicago-police" >Off-duty FBI agent fatally shot man who was firing into crowd in Pilsen, officials say</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/06/04/fbi-bank-robbery-tech-bmo-abdulhafedh-chicago" >FBI’s high-tech hunt led to killing of alleged bank robbery ‘mastermind’ in West Side shoot-out</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/19/shooting-fbi-atf-hotaling-boutros-country-club-hills" >Video contradicts FBI agent’s account of shooting during undercover sting in Country Club Hills</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>
