entries.title: Ebony/Jet building's lost, hip interiors detailed in new book
entries.summary: <p>Nearly a decade has gone by since the former Ebony/Jet Building was sold to a residential developer, and the most original, intact and supremely funky 1970s corporate interiors in the U.S. was lost.</p><p>Designed by Black Chicago architect John Moutoussamy and opening in 1972, the 11-story Johnson Publishing Company headquarters still retains its regal, modernist presence at 820 S. Michigan Ave.</p><p>However, the tower's insides — still abuzz and brimming with its original colors, patterns, textiles, materials and furnishings after 40 years — were wrecked and removed in 2017 to make way for 150 apartments.</p><p>Historic and one-of-a-kind spaces, gone forever. Another repeat of a Chicago story that's almost as old as the city itself.</p><p>But now, the Ebony/Jet interiors live again, courtesy of a new monograph published this month, "820 Ebony/Jet: Visions of the Johnson Publishing Company, an American Icon," by photographer Barbara Karant.</p><p>The book is a both a goodbye kiss and a loving remembrance to the historic Johnson Publishing offices, photographed between 2012 and 2015 — the years between the company's sale of the tower to Columbia College Chicago and developer 3L Real Estate's eventual purchase of the building from the liberal arts school.</p><p>The work features Karant's sharp, evocative images, plus well-written essays from those who either once worked in the building or studied its history. And including top-notch Ebony/Jet archival photos taken shortly after the building was opened and staffed is a very nice touch.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-d50000" name="image-d50000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/765bdc9/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1000x561+0+53/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fff%2Ffe%2F9e116abf4583b5af71c6a12d40fe%2Ffloor-10-12-barbara-karant.jpeg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7ed8000/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1000x561+0+53/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fff%2Ffe%2F9e116abf4583b5af71c6a12d40fe%2Ffloor-10-12-barbara-karant.jpeg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/83d5363/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1000x561+0+53/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fff%2Ffe%2F9e116abf4583b5af71c6a12d40fe%2Ffloor-10-12-barbara-karant.jpeg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="The 10th floor featured a glass door bearing the mod style Johnson Publishing Company logo. "I always felt that there was a lingering feeling of the company and what they did there and their creativity and energy within the space."</p><p>Founded by Black businessman John H. Johnson, Johnson Publishing was near its apex when it opened offices on South Michigan. The new building provided enough room for a growing corporate empire.</p><p>Its leading publication, the glossy monthly magazine Ebony, was entering its 26th year, and its weekly news digest, Jet, was class="Figure-credit"><p>Provided by Barbara Karant</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>And those 1972 interiors and virtually all of the original furnishing remained in the building — preserved, remade or restored — for 40 years until Johnson Publishing moved out in 2012.</p><p>"After Johnson Publishing Company moved out, I took a tour of the building," Karant, an adjunct photography professor at Columbia College, said. "I saw the space and by the time I was done touring it, I could barely construct a sentence because I was so completely enthralled."</p><p>I know the feeling. After I saw the interiors in 2013, <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/arts/2013/01/14/soul-survivor-a-look-at-the-intact-and-avant-garde-interiors-of-the-ebony-jet-building" target="_blank" >I wrote</a> the "offices embodied an Afrocentric modernism that was well-turned, avant-garde, and quite hip."</p><p>One space had leopard print carpet, Mozambique wood furnishings. Every floor in the building was different. And it was all unforgettable.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-940000" name="image-940000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7477c80/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4256x2389+0+222/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F38%2F02%2F6ac026594b02a2988747c1c2529a%2Febony-cst-1118-11.JPG 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/54f0faf/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4256x2389+0+222/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F38%2F02%2F6ac026594b02a2988747c1c2529a%2Febony-cst-1118-11.JPG 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/5b8f23b/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4256x2389+0+222/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F38%2F02%2F6ac026594b02a2988747c1c2529a%2Febony-cst-1118-11.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Exterior of Johnson Publishing Company's building at 820 S. entries.title: Dolores Huerta, influyente líder laboral, feminista e ícono de los derechos civiles, muere a los 96 años
entries.summary: <p>Dolores Huerta, quien cofundó el sindicato United Farm Workers para mejorar las condiciones laborales de los trabajadores en los campos de frutas y verduras del país y acuñó la frase "¡Sí se puede!", que se convirtió en un grito de lucha, ha fallecido a los 96 años.</p><p>La familia de Huerta dijo que falleció el miércoles en su casa.</p><p>“Sabemos que muchos de ustedes en todo el mundo comparten nuestro dolor, y estaremos informando sobre los planes para reconocer y celebrar su increíble vida y legado”, dijeron en un comunicado difundido por su fundación.</p><p>Huerta mantuvo una agenda apretada hasta entrados sus 90 años, marchando en protestas y ofreciendo discursos por todo el país sobre raza, pobreza, derechos LGBTQ+ y derechos de la mujer en nombre de su fundación con base en Bakersfield, California.</p><p>La firmeza de Huerta consolidó su lugar en la historia como una de las líderes laborales, figuras de los derechos civiles y activistas feministas más influyentes del país. Su eslogan de tres palabras “Sí se puede”—que se traduce como “Yes, we can”— se basaba en la creencia de que la gente que actúa puede generar cambios.</p><p>Su labor a lo largo de las décadas le concedió reconocimientos, entre ellos la Medalla Presidencial de la Libertad, el máximo honor civil del país. Cuando el presidente Barack Obama le entregó la condecoración en 2012, la elogió como una líder tenaz y reconoció que había tomado prestado su eslogan para su campaña de 2008.</p><p>Este año, Huerta sacudió a la comunidad latina al revelar que fue abusada sexualmente en la década de 1960 por el cofundador del movimiento de trabajadores agrícolas, César Chávez, lo que dio lugar al nacimiento de dos hijos, un secreto que había guardado durante 60 años, mucho después de la muerte de Chávez.</p><p>Desde principios de la década de 1970, su pareja de vida fue Richard Chávez, hermano de César, con quien tuvo cuatro hijos. También tuvo siete hijos de dos matrimonios anteriores.</p><p>Huerta dijo que había permanecido en silencio tanto tiempo porque temía que hablar comprometiera la obra de su vida y deshiciera todo el progreso logrado para los trabajadores.</p><p>Cuando le preguntaron durante una entrevista en 2026 con Latino USA sobre por qué guardó el secreto, Huerta dijo, “Era mi dolor personal, era mi problema personal y, ya saben, creo que valió la pena porque era mi cruz que cargar. Lo diré así”.</p><h4>Activismo nacido en casa</h4><p>Huerta nació como Dolores Clara Fernández en 1930 en Dawson, Nuevo México. Su padre era minero y activista sindical que llegó a ocupar un escaño en la Legislatura estatal. Sus padres se divorciaron cuando ella tenía 3 años, y su madre se llevó a Dolores y a sus hermanos a California.</p><p>Sumergida en un crisol de familias trabajadoras mexicanas, filipinas, afroamericanas, japonesas y chinas, Huerta aprendió de su madre —que era propietaria de un restaurante y un hotel— sobre la independencia, la compasión y el activismo.</p><p>Huerta era una joven y enérgica maestra de primaria en el valle agrícola de San Joaquín cuando decidió responder a otro llamado después de frustrarse por las malas condiciones de vida de sus alumnos.</p><p>“No podía soportar ver a los niños llegar a clase con hambre y necesitando zapatos”, dijo en 2017 en un documental de PBS Independent Lens sobre su vida. “Pensé que podía hacer más organizando a los trabajadores agrícolas que tratando de enseñarles a sus hijos con hambre”.</p><p>El trabajo inicial de Huerta con un grupo de derechos civiles en Stockton la llevó a conocer a Chávez. Ambos quisieron enfocarse más en la difícil situación de los trabajadores agrícolas, por lo que en 1962 fundaron la National Farm Workers Association, que años después se convirtió en United Farm Workers of America (UFW). Fue una líder clave y negociadora del sindicato durante años.</p><p>Estuvo entre quienes se unieron a recolectores de uvas filipinos en lo que se convirtió en la huelga de uvas de Delano que duró cinco años. Con Chávez, negoció contratos colectivos y acuerdos con grandes productores, logrando los primeros planes de salud y beneficios para los trabajadores agrícolas.</p><p>Chávez, quien murió en 1993, la describió en una ocasión como intrépida, comprometida con la causa y dura a la hora de negociar.</p><h4>En la campaña</h4><p>Conoció al senador Robert Kennedy, de Massachusetts, durante su visita a Delano en 1968 y trabajó como voluntaria en su campaña presidencial, registrando a mexicoamericanos en California para que votaran. Huerta estuvo en el escenario con Kennedy después de que él ganó las elecciones primarias de California y él la agradeció públicamente, momentos antes de ser asesinado.</p><p>El magnicidio devastó a Huerta, pero ella siguió organizando. Huerta fue encarcelada 22 veces por participar en protestas sindicales.</p><p>En 1988 sufrió heridas graves mientras protestaba por la oposición del candidato presidencial republicano George H.W. Bush al boicot de uvas de la UFW durante su visita a San Francisco.</p><p>Atrapada en una multitud, fue golpeada con un bastón por un policía, sufrió tres costillas fracturadas y un bazo destrozado, y requirió más de una docena de transfusiones de sangre. Alcanzó un acuerdo con la Ciudad para resolver sus reclamaciones.</p><p>Tras una larga recuperación, Huerta cambió de enfoque e inició una gira para hacer campaña por los derechos de la mujer e incentivar a las latinas a postularse a cargos públicos.</p><p>También hizo campaña por los presidentes demócratas Bill Clinton, Barack Obama y Joe Biden. El gobernador de California, Gavin Newsom, la consideraba una amiga cercana.</p><h4>Impulsada por el valor</h4><p>Emilio Huerta, uno de los 13 hijos de Dolores, dijo en una entrevista que la valentía de su madre impulsó la obra de su vida.</p><p>“Dedicar tu vida a construir el sueño de un sindicato para los trabajadores agrícolas, enfrentarse a la [industria de la] agricultura, que hasta hoy sigue siendo una potencia... Eso requirió mucho valor”, dijo.</p><p>Huerta aprendió el arte de presionar a los políticos, asegurar ayuda financiera para los desempleados y el seguro por discapacidad para los trabajadores agrícolas de California. Denunció el uso de pesticidas tóxicos, impulsó la amnistía para inmigrantes indocumentados y se opuso a programas federales de trabajadores invitados.</p><p>Al dirigir boicots nacionales de uvas y lechuga a principios de los años setenta, ayudó a crear la presión económica y el clima político necesarios para que California aprobara la primera ley estatal que reconocía el derecho de los trabajadores agrícolas a la negociación colectiva.</p><p>Entre sus numerosos reconocimientos, fue la primera latina incluida en el National Women’s Hall of Fame, y recibió nueve doctorados honoris causa de universidades estadounidenses. Escuelas en California, Texas y Colorado llevan su nombre. Su imagen adorna muchos murales y hay calles que la honran con su nombre.</p><p>Pero no siempre contó con el favor de los activistas más liberales.</p><p>En 2016, cuando respaldó a Hillary Rodham Clinton en lugar del senador Bernie Sanders en las primarias presidenciales demócratas, la actriz Rosario Dawson —partidaria de Sanders que interpretó a Huerta en una película de 2014 sobre César Chávez— dijo que Huerta se había convertido en “un instrumento del sistema”.</p><p>Dawson y Huerta finalmente se reconciliaron.</p><p>El guitarrista Carlos Santana supervisó después un documental basado en la vida de Huerta tras una conversación nocturna que ambos tuvieron sobre música mientras estaban en Hawái. Santana, fan de Miles Davis, descubrió que Huerta era una gran admiradora de la leyenda del bebop Charlie Parker.</p><p>“Incluso conocí a Charlie Parker. Esa es mi carta de presentación”, bromeó Huerta en una entrevista con la Associated Press cuando tenía 87 años.</p><p>El trabajo de Huerta como líder del movimiento obrero reverberó en Estados Unidos y más allá, haciendo su nombre sinónimo de derechos civiles. En el documental de 2025 “Seeds of Change: The Life and Legacy of Dolores Huerta”, contó sobre su activismo de décadas y dijo que la inspiración que obtuvo del movimiento de mujeres en los años setenta le dio la validación que necesitaba para subir al escenario con otros líderes sindicales.</p><p>“Espero que mi legado sea el de una organizadora que organizó para luchar contra la injusticia”, dijo en la película. “Les queremos dejar a nuestros hijos una herencia de justicia, de derecho, no de joyas o propiedades o dinero porque sólo se pelearán por eso. Así que lo principal es darles este amor por la justicia —y ese es el mayor regalo que creo que cualquiera de nosotros puede tener”.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" >La Voz Chicago</a><br></p>

entries.title: Bridgeport Bears? Chicago firm releases plans for glitzy new domed stadium at Sox park site
entries.summary: <p>A Chicago architectural firm on Wednesday released renderings of a plan that would put the Bears in a new domed stadium at the site of Bridgeport’s Rate Field — and potentially help bolster a plan for the Chicago White Sox to move to the South Loop.</p><p>Skidmore, Owings and Merrill posted the renderings to their Instagram page Wednesday, saying the plan would create a new home for the Bears in Bridgeport, with a mixed-use district that would bring together housing, entertainment, hospitality, parks and public recreation. The firm noted that the transportation infrastructure is already in place at the site, with access to the CTA, Metra and the Dan Ryan Expressway.</p> <p>Renderings of the plan that are being distributed to stakeholders say the stadium and campus is "presented by Sterling Bay." The architect who crafted the plan told the Sun-Times Skidmore is "not driving this deal although we love the idea of keeping the Bears in Chicago."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div large amount of publicly-owned land surrounding the site that could transform the stadium into a district with more affordable and market-rate housing, civic amenities and new and improved pedestrian bridges to bring lasting vitality to the surrounding neighborhoods,” the architectural firm said.</p><p>Sources said the plan would include moving Wentworth Gardens, a nearby housing development, which would certainly meet some resistance.</p><p>But a Bears stadium at the site, which is owned by the Illinois Sports Facilities Authority, could mean that the team could avoid paying property taxes, a major selling point. There’s also the built-in infrastructure, with the potential for federal transportation funds as well.</p><p>All of the chatter comes as Canal Edge LLC — a company owned by White Sox minority owner Justin Ishbia — released plans in September for a mixed-use development called The Railyards, which would <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/05/new-sox-park-future-owner-announces-proposal-for-riverside-stadium-at-the-railyards" >move the Chicago White Sox </a>to the South Loop. The stadium would sit alongside the Chicago River stretching from Roosevelt Road to the north to 18th Street to the south, and bordered with the river on its east side and Canal Street to its west.</p><p>The move came hand-in-hand with <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2025/06/06/justin-ishbia-white-sox-jerry-reinsdorf-ownership-winnetka" target="_blank" ><u>Ishbia</u></a>’s companies helping to finance Amtrak’s move while purchasing the existing rail facility, which it wants to develop as a site for a proposed new stadium for the South Side team.</p><p>That plan has met some major community resistance because Amtrak initially had received more than $600 million and a “<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/what-to-know-chicago-white-sox-stadium-proposal-justin-ishbia" target="_blank" ><u>categorical exclusion</u></a>” from the federal government for the project, which allowed it to move forward without a full environmental assessment or an environmental impact statement “unless there are extraordinary circumstances.”</p><p>However, the Federal Railroad Administration this week said Amtrak’s new proposed maintenance facility in Bridgeport would undergo a federal environmental review after community pushback.</p><p>Mayor Brandon Johnson's office on Wednesday offered up little details, saying in a statement to the Sun-Times that “the Mayor knows that Chicago is and should remain the home of the Bears and will continue to work with stakeholders across the region to do so.”</p><p>Bridgeport Ald. Nicole Lee (11th) said she is intrigued by the possibility of having the Bears replace the Sox on site that now includes Guaranteed Rate Field, even though there are more far more questions than answers about the 11th-hour plan. Lee and Cook County Commissioner John Daley have been embroiled in the battle with Amtrak Ishbia to prevent the Sox from leaving Rate Field for the South Loop. That plan also entails the construction of the Amtrak maintenance site in Bridgeport.</p><p>“I’m absolutely interested in conversations about what’s possible on this land — especially because the Sox haven’t necessarily talked to us about what it would take for them to stay. So, I think that’s a great conversation to be having,” Lee said Wednesday.</p><p>“The plans are — they’re real pretty pictures. But there’s still a lot we need to have extensive conversations about.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a built by the Illinois Sports Facilities Authority (ISFA) and bankrolled by an increase in the hotel tax. Another $50 million in outstanding stadium authority bonds were used to fund a renovation of the Sox stadium and won’t be retired until 2029, when the Sox lease there expires.</p><p>Lee said she is “glad that people are looking at the ISFA property as something that has great potential, which is something that we’ve been saying for a long time.”</p><p>It’s not the first time that a Chicago developer and its handpicked stadium architect has showcased dazzling stadium renderings.</p><p>“Pretty pictures” have accompanied plans to build a Bears stadium at the site that once housed Michael Reese Hospital, and the plan once championed by Sox Chairman Jerry Reinsdorf to build a new Sox stadium at the South Loop parcel known as “the 78.” That’s where the Chicago Fire’s billionaire owner, Joe Mansueto, is financing his own $750 million soccer stadium with help from $425 million in taxpayer-funded infrastructure improvements.</p><p>Both of those earlier stadium plans have, so far, gone Asked whether she believes the plan to build a Bears stadium in Bridgeport is real, or more like a Hail Mary pass, Lee answered, “I don’t know. I have not had any conversations with the Bears at all about a potential move to our area.”</p><p>“It’s interesting the timing of everything right now knowing that Sterling Bay is also working with the Canal Edge folks as well with regards to the rail yards,” the company owned by Ishbia.</p><p>Lee said she looks forward to talking to stadium developers about “what’s possible on 35th Street…That’s gonna need to involve the state because the state owns all of that property.”</p><p>“Different here than with the Amtrak maintenance facility, this land is in a planned development and it would be subject to all of the city’s planned development requirements. So, we’re a long way off,” Lee said. “The timing is interesting, and the players are interesting.”</p><p>Lee said she has long found it strange that the Bears stadium search has dominated the public conversation and political debate even though the team’s lease at Soldier Field does not expire until 2033.</p><p>“The fact that the Sox lease is coming due sooner was a little frustrating,” she said. “I’m happy that there’s at least some other conversations going on about what the future of all of these teams is.”</p><p>If the Skidmore plan ever does take off, Lee said, “They’re gonna be building a whole complex and there are some things that would need to come down” and be demolished. She refused to reveal specifics. “That is why this is so far away from being real,” she said.</p><p>Gov. JB Pritzker has been driving talks as of late, meeting again last month with <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium/2026/10/01/nfl-commissioner-roger-goodell-illinois-visit-bears-stadium-talks-gov-jb-pritzker" >NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell,</a> whose repeated visits to Illinois might suggest the league’s not thrilled at the prospect of breaking ground on a Hammond dome.</p><p>Pritzker has supported the broader concept of allowing the Bears to negotiate a discounted payment in lieu of taxes, known as PILOT, with local governments. The Illinois House passed such a bill this spring, earning critical support from Chicago Democrats because it would’ve shared proceeds with homeowners as property tax rebates — but those returns were deemed “<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium/2026/05/04/bears-stadium-property-tax-relief-pritzker-negligible" target="_blank" ><u>negligible</u></a>.”</p><p>In the Illinois General Assembly, sources familiar with the negotiations say the conversation has shifted toward the stadium authority model. That would mean no tax bill for the Bears — and it’d keep the door open to Chicago, providing vital cover for city legislators loath to pave the team’s path to Arlington Heights.</p><div entries.title: Bears report: Injured Coby Bryant progressing but without an exact return date
entries.summary: <p><b>Coby Bryant Update</b><br>Ben Johnson is keeping it vague on Coby Bryant. He said the safety is progressing through rehab but didn’t have an exact timeline for returning.</p><p>“From what I understand, he's right on track,” Johnson said. “He's working his tail off…Over the next month, that'll go a long way to see whether we can get him back this year or not.”</p><p>According to Johnson, Bryant will begin running on land in the "near future," but practicing change of direction will reveal more about his trajectory.</p><p>“We're still a little ways away from him doing the change of direction stuff,” Johnson said. “That's really going to be the stress test with him is being able to really push down on that knee and change direction at a high velocity. So that's still a little ways away."</p><p><b>Attendance</b><br>Cornerbacks Malik Muhammad II (toe) and Tyrique Stevenson Sr. (hamstring) were both absent from practice Wednesday. Linebackers T.J. Edwards (hamstring) and Jack Sanborn (concussion) returned.</p><p><b>Loveland on Kmet </b><br>Coleston Loveland is feeling the loss of fellow tight-end Cole Kmet, who will miss the rest of the season with a knee injury.</p><p>“He’s a strong guy and he’s going to get through it for sure,” Loveland said. “I love that guy. He’s done so much for me and taught me so much and someone I look up to.</p><p>“You can’t replace a guy like that, but we got other guys that can step up and we all just need to do a little bit more."</p>

entries.title: Why do we elect people to manage our wastewater?
entries.summary: <p>Every time Chicagoans flush a toilet, run a sink or prepare for a heavy downpour, they rely on the work of an agency many may know little about: the Metropolitan Water Reclamation District of Greater Chicago. This November, voters will elect four commissioners to the district’s nine-member board, which oversees wastewater treatment and prevents flooding across Cook County. </p><p>Here’s what the agency does and what’s at stake in the election.</p><h3>What does the Metropolitan Water Reclamation District of Greater Chicago do?</h3><p>The MWRD treats wastewater from homes and businesses before releasing the cleaned water back into the environment. It also manages stormwater to reduce flooding and protect waterways from pollution.</p><p>The agency was established in 1889 as the Sanitary District of Chicago because sewage from the Chicago River was contaminating Lake Michigan, the city’s drinking-water source. The district helped reverse the river’s flow by building the Chicago Sanitary and Ship Canal, directing wastewater away from the lake.</p><p>Today, the MWRD treats wastewater at seven plants serving Chicago and 128 surrounding communities. Much of the city's wastewater is treated at the Stickney Water Reclamation Plant before flowing into waterways and eventually reaching the Mississippi River and the Gulf of Mexico.</p><h3>Who runs the MWRD? Who is on the board?</h3><p>The district is governed by a nine-member Board of Commissioners. Commissioners are elected countywide in Cook County, rather than representing individual city wards or districts.</p><p>The board oversees the agency’s policies, budget and major decisions. Commissioners serve staggered six-year terms, so not all nine seats are on the ballot in the same election.</p><p>The district is independent of Chicago and Cook County governments. Its work is funded primarily through property taxes, making commissioners responsible for overseeing substantial public spending. The district’s 2026 budget included $755.7 million in property taxes. Its 2027 budget recommendations project $782.4 million, according to the district’s budget dashboard.</p><h3>Which seats are up for election in November 2026?</h3><p>There are four MWRD commissioner seats on the Nov. 3 ballot: three regular six-year terms and one two-year term to finish an unexpired term.</p><ul class="rte2-style-ul" style="margin-top:0;margin-bottom:0;padding-inline-start:48px;" id="rte-2fe659a0-d2f2-11f1-9ea3-13615c4bc7af"><li>Six-year terms: Incumbents Eira Corral Sepúlveda, Precious Brady-Davis and Beth McElroy Kirkwood are running for reelection against Republican candidates Michelle Pennington, Timothy E. Rueckert and Jill B. Shestokas.</li><li>Two-year term: Incumbent Cameron “Cam” Davis is running unopposed to complete the remaining two years of a term.<br></li></ul><h3>How does the election work? How many candidates can voters choose?</h3><p>Cook County voters can select up to three candidates for the regular six-year seats. The three candidates who receive the most votes win those seats.</p><p>The two-year seat is a separate race, with Davis running unopposed.</p><h3>What are the MWRD’s biggest challenges?</h3><p>Flooding and infrastructure are major challenges. The district operates the Tunnel and Reservoir Plan, known as the Deep Tunnel, which stores excess stormwater and wastewater during heavy rain, until it can be treated, instead of overflowing into waterways.</p><p>But the system has limits. In July, after days of heavy rain, the McCook Reservoir reached between 96% and 100% capacity, while the Thornton Reservoir reached 94%, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2026/07/06/chicago-deep-tunnel-historic-flooding-tarp-reservoir-weather-climate-change" target="_blank" >as reported by the Sun-Times.</a> The reservoirs’ limited remaining capacity raised flood risks in nearby communities and sewage overflows entered the Chicago River.</p><p>The July flooding underscored the limits of the region’s existing infrastructure, even with billions of dollars invested in the Deep Tunnel system over several decades. As the MWRD continues expanding that system and managing increasingly heavy rainfall, the elected commissioners will be charged with shaping how the district responds to such future challenges.</p>
entries.author: Misha Manjuran Oberoi

entries.title: Man posed as basketball coach to sexually abuse boy, 15, police say
entries.summary: <p>A Far South Side man is accused of posing as a basketball coach in order to sexually abuse a 15-year-old earlier this year, Chicago police said Wednesday. </p><p>Andre D. Jackson, 56, was charged with indecent solicitation/aggravated criminal sexual abuse and grooming, both of which are felonies, police said. </p><p>Jackson, of West Pullman, was arrested Monday after being identified as the person who, over several months earlier this year, "presented himself as a basketball coach and proceeded to commit acts of indecent solicitation and grooming of a 15-year-old boy," police said in a statement. </p><p>Jackson was scheduled for a detention hearing Wednesday. </p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: DOJ to send election monitors to Northwest Indiana
entries.summary: <p>Ella Kelly usually votes early, but she’s especially happy she got it done Tuesday.</p><p>The grandmother from Gary, Indiana, visited the Lake County Government Complex in Crown Point to cast her ballot a week before the Nov. 3 midterm election.</p><p>“It’s much more convenient,” Kelly said. “That’s why I’ve been voting like this for the past five years.”</p><p>The Department of Justice informed state officials it plans to send election monitors to polling places in two majority-Democratic counties. Besides Lake County, in Northwest Indiana, it will also will send the monitors to Marion County, home to the capital, Indianapolis.</p><p>In a statement, the department announced that nationwide, it will have about 1,000 monitors in place to monitor for potential violations to federal law, which will be reviewed after election day. It called the monitoring "routine," but the announcement concerns some Democratic officials as well as some residents, including Kelly.</p><p>“I think it’s a scare tactic; it’s a form of intimidation,” Kelly said. “It’s a way of controlling people and causing trouble.”</p><p>Lake and Marion counties are historically blue areas in a mostly-red state, <a class="Link" href="https://enr.indianavoters.in.gov/archive/2024General/index.html" target="_blank" >and in 2024 both were carried by Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris</a> — in Marion County, Harris' margin was nearly 28 percentage points.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-250000" entries.title: Mayoral challenger Susana Mendoza vows to repair 'damaged relationship' between City Hall and business
entries.summary: <p>Mayoral challenger Susana Mendoza vowed Wednesday to repair what she called the “damaged” relationship between City Hall and Chicago’s business community by treating business “as a partner — not a piggy bank.”</p><p>Two days after filing her nomination petitions to join the now 15-candidate field seeking to deny Mayor Brandon Johnson a second term, Mendoza portrayed the embattled incumbent as openly hostile to business.</p><p>During a luncheon address to the City Club of Chicago, Mendoza pointed to the proposed $17.6 billion budget that will serve as Johnson’s re-election platform.</p><p>“The mayor’s proposed head tax — it kills jobs by penalizing companies for hiring more Chicagoans. His push to borrow another $480 million saddles us with more high-interest debt that we cannot afford. His personal property lease transaction tax stifles tech ecosystem growth and drives up everyday costs, from ride shares to streaming service,” Mendoza said.</p><p>“We must grow our economy — not tax it into further decline.”</p><p>Illinois Secretary of State Alexi Giannoulias, U.S. Rep. Mike Quigley, Cook County Board of Review Commissioner George Cardenas and Cook County Treasurer Maria Pappas are all running for re-election to their current office while campaigning for mayor. Mendoza chose to retire as state comptroller to mount her second mayoral campaign.</p><p>On Wednesday, she told the City Club audience of movers and shakers her “growth plan” for Chicago’s economy starts with “re-setting the City Hall relationship with the business community and the markets.”</p><p>The longstanding partnership forged between City Hall, labor and business “guided us through disasters and downturns that flattened” other cities “by choosing collaboration over combat when it mattered most,” but those days are over, Mendoza said.</p><p>“The relationship between City Hall and the business community has been damaged. I will restore it,” Mendoza said to applause.</p><p></p><p></p><p>Mendoza said she would measure the success of her growth plan against five big-picture goals: reducing the cost of living; rapid construction of new housing; population gains; “ramping up job creation in every neighborhood" and “leading in key emerging industries shaping the next economy.”</p><p>She promised “sustained housing construction and population growth" would be underway in her first term.</p><p></p><p>“As mayor, I will make the construction crane the official bird of Chicago," she said. "We’re gonna see more cranes than pigeons."</p><p></p><p></p><p></p><p></p><p>And within eight years — "which means you have to vote for me twice," she joked — Mendoza vowed to "transform" workforce development and job creation "in every neighborhood" of Chicago.</p><p>"Black unemployment in this city is unreasonably high — and we do not talk about it enough. Addressing it will be one of my top priorities as your mayor," she said.</p><p></p><p>Mendoza promised to "connect training in every neighborhood directly to employer needs," measure success by how many Chicagoans "secure good-paying jobs" and create a "robust program to lower costs for small businesses," she said.</p><p>"Chicago businesses deserve to stop feeling like piggy banks and start feeling like partners."</p><p></p><p></p>

entries.title: Mayor Johnson under fire for shrinking CPD
entries.summary: <p>Civic Federation President Joe Ferguson has accused Mayor Brandon Johnson of “chopping away” at the Chicago Police Department to help balance his pre-election budget after three years of shrinking CPD by attrition, but the mayor apparently wanted to go further.</p><p>Acting Police Superintendent Fred Waller told the City Council Wednesday he negotiated with the mayor’s office to keep the police academy going year-round.</p><p> At Waller's request, the mayor agreed to keep the training going for 12 months, with recruit classes of “50 or more,” he said.</p><p>Waller disclosed the mayoral concession during day-long testimony at City Council budget hearings. </p><p> The mayor’s $17.6 billion budget already is under attack for freezing 368 police vacancies and replacing dozens of additional police officers with civilians. </p><p>“The budget your department has been handed by this administration … has shown a steady decline in budgeted police officer positions,” downtown Ald. Brendan Reilly (42nd) told Waller during Council budget hearings.</p><p>“In 2024, 833 police officer positions were eliminated. In 2025, a net 54 officer positions were cut. Last year, only six were added back. This budget eliminates 132 more positions. Did the department ask for these reductions?”</p><p>Waller replied: “Well, in negotiation for this year, the mayor’s office asked for those 132 positions. But we also negotiated for — instead of just having academy classes for about eight months of the year — we were given academy classes of 50 or more for the whole twelve months” of 2027.</p><p>“That will allow us to catch up and have more robust recruitment,” he said.</p><p>Last year, CPD hired 539 officers and lost 397 cops to retirement. So far this year, there have been 407 hirings and 363 retirements. The department is barely keeping pace with attrition.</p><p>“Recruitment is always a challenge right now for how many officers we actually need,” Waller said. “When I was chief of patrol, I think we had about 14,000 officers, somewhere in that number, give or take maybe 1,000 or so. So we've lost a lot.” </p><p>Response times have suffered most in South and West Side police districts where violent crime has traditionally been highest.</p><p>Finance Chair Pat Dowell (3rd) asked what the mayor’s hiring freeze would do to the already gaping difference in response times between districts, and to the time available to devote to community policing.</p><p>“We share the same concerns looking at the trends” in response times, said First Deputy Police Superintendent Antoinette Ursitti.</p><p>“We're looking district by district, and then digging in even deeper to look watch by watch to see where, if at all, there's bottlenecks and what we can be doing to support that.”</p><p>Pointing to the push to civilianize police jobs, Ursitti said, “Officers who are able to do essential duties like respond to a call for service — if they’re in a role right now where that can be fulfilled by a non-sworn member — we’re making that change." </p><p>North Side Ald. Timmy Knudsen (43rd) had a more immediate concern: The rash of burglaries hitting businesses along Clark Street. Thirteen windows were smashed on Monday night alone.</p><p>“A pretty low amount of cash. A pretty senseless crime. Damage to the business is usually a higher dollar amount than the cash that the burglars can get. I know this is happening citywide,” Knudsen said, demanding to know the department’s “strategic response.”</p><p>Chief of Detectives Kevin Bruno argued that retail burglary investigations are “challenging” because they traditionally involve “off-hours” break-ins by “masked offenders in stolen vehicles.”</p><p>Bruno promised to “build those investigations through video, through license plate readers, through cell phone data — all of that to track down, identify and disrupt these burglary crews.”</p><p>Knudsen complained the number of officers assigned to the Near North and Town Hall Districts is down “quite significantly.”</p><p>“It’s really hard to compete with the demands of downtown in the south part of my ward. And up north, there’s nights where officers will be all around Wrigley Field and we can’t get one patrol car down to the north part of my ward,” Knudsen said.</p><p>When pressed for information on a long-awaited replacement for ShotSpotter, police department officials refused to provide specifics or name the winner of the ongoing bid process.</p><p>Officials also appeared to know little about a pilot program that includes gun detection technology and is launching across the city.</p><p>Dan Casey with the Office of Public Safety Administration told Ald. Matt O’Shea (19th) to direct pilot-related questions to the mayor’s chief procurement officer, who announced the program in a letter last week.</p><p>“So let's just let the cat out of the bag,” O’Shea said. “We need procurement here, or we need the mayor's office.”</p><p></p><p></p>

entries.title: Blackhawks' attendance pacing above last season so far, but fans won't stay patient forever
entries.summary: <p>Declining attendance has been a hot-button topic around the NHL in recent weeks, and the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a> have been cited as one of several relevant examples.</p><p>A sparse crowd of 15,028 on Oct. 15 against the Jets — the Hawks' smallest in more than three years — was what really got national attention.</p><p>But through the Hawks' first eight home games this season, their overall attendance is actually up from last year. They've averaged 17,926 tickets distributed per game, compared to 17,324 through their first eight home games last season.</p><p>They sold out their home opener, which didn't happen last year, and they nearly sold out Oct. 23 against the Canadiens, as well.</p><p>Plus, that Jets game marks the only time they've fallen below 16,000 so far — something that happened twice last October. Their home-stand finale <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/10/27/blackhawks-wyatt-kaiser-kings-goals-gap-control" >Tuesday</a> against the Kings seemed a likely candidate to end up in the 15,000s (or worse), but strong day-of ticket sales lifted it to a respectable 16,437.</p><p>October is always the most difficult month for NHL teams to sell tickets, but it's worth noting the difference was particularly dramatic for the Hawks last season.</p><p>Attendance rose sharply around the Thanksgiving and Christmas holidays and remained pretty strong throughout the second half of the season. That ticked their final average all the way up to 18,949 per game, which ranked fifth in the NHL and set a new post-pandemic <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/04/16/blackhawks-attendance-ticket-sales-centennial-rewarding-fans" >high-water mark</a> for the Hawks.</p><p>So if attendance doesn't rise as sharply this season, the Hawks could fall behind last season's pace. They still have five more home games to get through — four of which fall on weeknights — before Thanksgiving arrives, and they have fewer December home games than usual due to their Germany trip.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-e20000" name="image-e20000"></a> <picture </div> </div><p>Around the league, the ends of the Golden Knights' and Oilers' sellout streaks have gotten lots of publicity, sparking conversations about franchises pricing out loyal fans in uncertain economic times.</p><p>The Devils and Canucks (unsurprisingly) have also seen attendance declines compared to this time last year, while the Sabres have ridden their long-awaited playoff berth last spring to join the league's sellout-every-night tier.</p><p>In Chicago, prices have certainly increased over the years — not only for tickets but also for concessions and parking, the latter being a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/10/20/blackhawks-united-center-parking-changes-prices-construction" >hot-button topic</a> in part because of steep price increases enforced by the United Center.</p><p>I would argue fan sentiment toward the on-ice product currently poses a stronger threat to Hawks attendance than prices do, though.</p><p>The timing of the Hawks' Centennial Season last season was advantageous for the team's sales department. All of the special events, alumni appearances and advertising around the city provided insurance against fan fatigue toward losing; big crowds were essentially guaranteed for a number of games.</p><p>With the Connor Bedard novelty factor having worn off and the Centennial festivities concluded, this season initially seemed like a make-or-break point for the Hawks to start wooing fans with genuine on-ice improvement. </p><p>The excitement surrounding Patrick Kane's return evidently bought them a little more time, however, considering attendance has remained passable despite the team's poor start (although they are 4-4 at home vs. 0-4 on the road).</p><p>Perhaps now that make-or-break point has been pushed to the spring, or to 2027-28. Regardless, it's coming eventually. </p><p>The great size and devotion of the Hawks' fan base made this long rebuild economically viable from the start — it wouldn't have been in smaller markets — but the franchise can only exploit those things for so long.</p><p>They owe it to fans to start delivering a better product soon. If they don't, the consequences will become increasingly visible when looking around the United Center. </p><p>I believe the Hawks do vividly understand that (at all levels of the organization), but it's now a matter of actually making it happen.</p>

entries.title: School board member was suspended from charter job after ‘unwanted touching’ of co-worker, records show
entries.summary: <p>A candidate running for reelection in a heated Chicago School Board race was suspended from his job at a charter school in 2018 after an investigation by the charter school operator found he became intoxicated at a work event and acted inappropriately with a co-worker, according to a letter obtained by the Chicago Sun-Times.</p><p>The letter, sent to Carlos Rivas Jr. by the Noble Network of Charter Schools in September 2018, says an internal investigation found that Rivas engaged in “unwanted touching of another employee without consent” in violation of Noble’s harassment policy during an event at The Robey Chicago hotel in August 2018.</p><p>Rivas was intoxicated “to the extent that, by his own admission” he could not deny the allegations due to “an inability to remember” what happened that evening, according to the letter. Rivas was an alumni support and external affairs manager at UIC College Prep at the time.</p><p>The 2018 investigation and its findings are surfacing less than a week before voters head to the polls on Nov. 3 and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/09/21/what-you-need-to-know-about-chicagos-historic-school-board-election" target="_blank" ><u>elect all 21 members of the school board</u></a> for the first time.</p><p>Rivas, who represents the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/school-board/districts/3b/" target="_blank" ><u>Northwest Side District 3b</u></a>, is trying to fend off challenger Jason Dónes, who is backed by the Chicago Teachers Union. Our Schools, a political action committee funded by the CTU, is distributing mailers highlighting the investigation and urging voters to oppose Rivas. The group has spent about $20,000 supporting Dónes’ candidacy as of the end of September.</p><p>Rivas said it was “disappointing” to see the issue resurface so close to the election.</p><p>“This was eight years ago, during an incredibly difficult period while caring for my mother, who was suffering from end-stage renal failure and dementia,” Rivas said in a statement. “I took responsibility, received support through Noble’s Employee Assistance program, and continued serving students and families at Noble for another four years.</p><p>“That experience is part of why I’ve championed mental health support for school employees on the board of education,” Rivas continued. “I believe in accountability, growth and second chances. I’m proud of my record and remain focused on the students and families of District 3b.”</p><p>According to the 2018 letter, Noble had previously warned Rivas about getting intoxicated at work-related events.</p><p>Rivas agreed to stipulations for “one last chance” to continue working at the charter school, the letter states. That included a 10-day suspension without pay, abstaining from “intoxicating substances” while working or at work-related events and seeking counseling through the charter operator’s employee assistance program.</p><p>“Failure to meet the terms of this agreement, to make improvement, or recurrence of any inappropriate behavior or conduct will result in immediate termination,” the letter states.</p><p>Rivas kept his position at Noble until 2022 when became public affairs director for the Civilian Office of Police Accountability, a position he still holds. Noble didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.</p><p>Rivas ran for school board in 2024, where he also faced off against Dónes, and won with 54% of the vote. While on the board Rivas has taken a fiscally conservative approach to the school budget. He was one of six school board members who voted against passing a <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/chicago-school-board/2026/07/30/chicago-school-board-approves-budget-that-reverses-layoffs-but-counts-on-shaky-state-funds" target="_blank" ><u>budget that included uncommitted revenue</u></a> from the state.</p><p>In this year’s election, Rivas is supported by the Service Employees International Union Illinois State Council, which represents thousands of CPS school support staff. He is also endorsed by the Common Ground Collective, a political action committee that is heavily funded by billionaire Michael Sacks and has taken opposing stances to that of the CTU.</p><p>Both men grew up in Humboldt Park and identify as progressives.</p><p>Schools in District 3b are struggling with teacher and counselor shortages, higher property taxes and low enrollment amid rapid gentrification and neighborhood changes.</p><p><i>Contributing: Ariel Parrella-Aureli of Block Club Chicago</i></p>

entries.title: Women's sports bars rally for WNBA Final after schedule change. 'This would never happen in men's sports.'
entries.summary: <p>Sorry, ladies. Prime time is for the boys. </p><p>Because of a scheduling conflict, the NBA moved Thursday's Game 6 of the WNBA Finals hours earlier so a regular season NBA game can tip off in the evening at Atlanta's State Farm Arena.</p><p>Now the Golden State Valkyries and the Atlanta Dream face off at 11:30 a.m. CT. </p><p>To accommodate the unusually early start time, at least three of Chicago's women's sports bars plan to open well before their normal hours so that fans can watch the game. </p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/p/DfAZ6KBifJD/" target="_blank" >Babe’s Sports Bar</a> in Logan Square will open at 9 a.m., <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/p/DfC6drioRV4/?hl=en" target="_blank" >Level Sporting Club</a> in Lake View will open at 11 a.m. and <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/p/De-PUO1MlgE/?hl=en" target="_blank" >Whiskey Girl Tavern</a> in Edgewater will open at the start of the game. </p><p>"We are gong to prove that even if you try to f*** with us, we're still going to make this work," said Nora McConnell-Johnson, the owner of Babe's. </p><p>McConnell-Johnson is opening her bar early under a temporary rebrand: Babe's Cafe. The bar will serve drip coffee from New Wave Coffee, matcha lattes made by one of Babe's bartenders and homemade McGriddles. </p><p>"In the women's sports world, you're used to a lot of last-minute changes because it's so often dismissed. But this is a new low that shocked even us," McConnell-Johnson said. "This would never happen in men's sports."</p><p>The Valkyries are up in the best-of-seven series 3-2 against the Dream. If Golden State wins, they take home their first championship. If Atlanta wins, they push the Valkyries to a deciding Game 7.</p><p>Their game was originally scheduled to tip off at 7 p.m. CT. But that conflicted with the Atlanta Hawks playing the Cleveland Cavaliers an hour earlier, also at State Farm Arena. </p><p>Atlanta Dream's owners claim they flagged the scheduling conflict two months ago, but say the NBA ignored their concerns. Meanwhile, the NBA claims moving the Hawks game would violate league rules that require teams to have at least 22 hours between consecutively scheduled games.</p><p>Despite the earlier start time, the Atlanta Dream sold out the 17,000-seat arena. As of Wednesday afternoon, plenty of seats are still for sale for the Hawks-Cavaliers game, according to ticket retailers Ticketmaster and SeatGeek. </p><p>McConnell-Johnson expects her bar to be packed for the game Thursday. Babe's has been full for the championship games so far, and they were counting on that revenue for Game 6. The bar, which opened in September 2025, turned a profit in its first year, McConnell-Johnson said. </p><p>"Women’s sports is good business. When you invest, you see great returns. When you don't, you're leaving money on the table," she said. </p><p>Clarissa Flores, owner of Level Sporting Club, shared McConnell-Johnson's sentiments. Changing the game's start time hurts the players, fans and small businesses like hers that depend on bumps in revenue from championship games, she said. </p><p>"It's disrespectful to the fans, it's disrespectful to the athletes, it's disrespectful to the teams," Flores says. She opened her bar five months ago with financial backing from several female athletes. </p><p>She also expects her bar to be packed. Her staff reworked their schedules to come in and supporters from the community have volunteered to help out. </p><p>"We’ll be sold out tomorrow," Flores said. "Why? Because the community is turning out for women’s basketball." </p>

entries.title: Bears look to bust slump in rushing attack as Seahawks' dominant defense looms Monday
entries.summary: <p>It says a lot about how much coach Ben Johnson elevated <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >the Bears</a>’ rushing attack that they’re in a three-week slump and still rank first in the NFL.</p><p>They’ve mostly gotten by regardless, thanks to quarterback Caleb Williams coming in hot off his injury, but they can’t count on that Monday when they visit the defending champion Seahawks. Every part of the offense needs to click to have a chance against that defense.</p><p>The Seahawks are elite at all three levels of their defense and are No. 6 against the run. They just held the Chiefs to a season-low 50 yards rushing, and 14 of that came from Patrick Mahomes.</p><p>That puts a lot on the Bears’ offensive line and lead running back <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/01/02/bears-rb-dandre-swift-adapted-to-new-scheme-hard-coaching-and-is-delivering-best-season-of-career" >D’Andre Swift</a>, who already is trending toward the most carries of his career.</p><p>“The front seven is one of the best in the league,” Swift said. “They play with a high level of energy and speed at all positions. We’ve got our work cut out for ourselves. That’s a great defense, but everyone here accepts that challenge.”</p><p>Swift ripped the Panthers for 124 yards and three touchdowns in the season opener, but hasn’t cracked 100 in a game since. The Bears’ 295 yards rushing against the Packers, Falcons and Patriots is their worst three-game stretch under Johnson since early last season.</p><p>The slump lines up with No. 2 running back Kyle Monangai’s absence due to a toe injury. Last time he was on the field, he rushed for 146 yards and two touchdowns against the Jets. In his absence, the Bears have given Roschon Johnson a tryout in that role, and this week they signed practice-squad back Zavier Scott to the active roster.</p><p>Monangai wasn’t on the field Wednesday during the portion of practice open to the media.</p><p>Nonetheless, the Bears have run for 154.3 yards per game this season, which puts them on pace for a top-10 rushing season in franchise history. That number was nearly 200 per game before the slump, and getting back to that potency is a priority.</p><p>There’s a good chance, too, that this game will be decided by whichever team runs the ball better.</p><p>It’s hard to even pick which part of the Seahawks’ defense is the strongest, but it might be their secondary. That group is good enough to keep tabs on the Bears’ skill players and frustrate Williams, so a steady run game is essential. The fewer passes the Bears leave out there for players like cornerback Devon Witherspoon and safety Julian Love, the better.</p><p>On the other side, Seahawks quarterback Sam Darnold has thrown an NFL-high eight interceptions and is playing his worst football of the last three seasons, which could tilt them toward the ground game. Plus, they might be getting rookie running back Jadarian Price back.</p><p>Price, a first-round pick from Notre Dame, has been on injured reserve with a chest injury, but is eligible to return Monday. He’s been practicing, and coach Mike MacDonald said it’s possible he’ll be ready to play.</p><p>“I saw his first three games, and he’s a good a player,” Bears linebacker Devin Bush said. “He was a first-round pick for a reason, but we haven’t seen much of him, so we’ve got to respect what’s on film right now and go off of that.”</p><p>The Seahawks also could get a boost from eight-time Pro Bowl guard Quenton Nelson, who came aboard this week in a trade with the Colts. MacDonald was similarly noncommittal about him being up to speed to play Monday.</p><p>The flashiness of Johnson’s pass plays makes it easy to forget that he’s a run-first coach at heart, so when he says “there’s a lot more to be had” in the ground game, there’s no doubt he spent his long weekend obsessing over ways to get it rolling again, even if the next opponent is the Seahawks.</p>
entries.author: Jason Lieser

entries.title: After humiliating Patrick Mahomes, Seahawks turn sights on Bears QB Caleb Williams
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> quarterback <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/10/28/bears-quarterback-caleb-williams-caddix-cleats-nfl-fine-keeping-wearing" target="_blank" >Caleb Williams</a> likes to hum on the sideline.</p><p>That, combined with his focus on deep breathing, helps him to relax. He’s been doing it for years.</p><p>“It’s calming,” he said of humming. “It calms your nervous system.”</p><p>The Seahawks, though, are really humming. And that can’t be relaxing for the Bears quarterback in the least.</p><p>Mike Macdonald's defense is coming off one of the most impressive defensive performances of the NFL season, a 20-3 “Sunday Night Football” shellacking of the Chiefs. </p><p>The Seahawks forced Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes into — Deep breaths, everybody —the worst game of his career. The three points the Chiefs scored in Seattle matched the lowest in his 153-game NFL career. For the first time with Mahomes under center, the Chiefs didn’t have a completion of at least 20 yards or a run of at least 10. They didn’t reach the red zone for the first time with Mahomes at quarterback.</p><p>The undefeated Chiefs were smothered to the tune of 11 first downs. Five of the Chiefs’ eight possessions produced one first down or fewer. Only one drive went for more than 50 yards. Mahomes went 19-for-33 for just 165 yards and one interception.</p><p>“Obviously that’s the best defense in football right now,” Williams said Wednesday. “Stats-wise and [with] players and scheme."</p><p>After the game, Chiefs coach Andy Reid said he’d take responsibility for not “putting guys in the right position to make plays,” saying it was time to go back to the drawing board.</p><p>A team that began the game undefeated ended it bewildered.</p><p>“The biggest takeaway,” Mahomes said, “is if you don't come ready to play, just you can get your tail kicked in this league.”</p><p>Toss out a seven-second drive at the end of the first half and four incompletions at the end of the game with the Chiefs down by 17, and they only had six series to run their actual offense.</p><p>“You look up at the end of the game and you have three points,” Bears coach Ben Johnson said of watching film of the game. “And it's like, ‘Holy cow, where did it all go wrong?’</p><p>“So I think it's one of those things that when you play a good team like this -- which, this is a really good team that's really well-coached -- and we're on the road, we're going to need the best out of everybody.”</p><p>Williams is at the top of that list. The last time the Bears played a top-shelf defense, Williams managed to score just three points against the Vikings on a rainy Soldier Field track in Week 2. He had a 56.2 passer rating and took three sacks before hurting his hamstring late in the fourth quarter.</p><p>Williams’ performance needs to rise along with the quality of his opponent.</p><p>“They don’t allow deep plays, so you’ve got to be as patient as possible,” Williams said. “That’s obviously hard the whole game trying to be patient, patient, patient. So it’s a challenge for me.</p><p>“It’s a challenge for our offense being able to take the dirty yards, protecting the football. They do a good job with punching the ball out and interceptions. … They rally to the ball. They got players. They got the scheme.”</p><p>The Seahawks give up the fewest yards in the league — and also the fewest passing yards. The 17.9 points per game they allow is the fourth-fewest in the NFL. Only the Packers have taken the ball away more than the Seahawks. Their eight interceptions trail just the Packers, too.</p><p>The Seahawks are able to rush the quarterback with just four players, Johnson said, which makes it hard for play-callers to get receivers open. They “do a phenomenal job taking away explosive plays in the passing game,” Johnson said, which forces teams to try to stay on schedule, march slowly down the field and score from the red zone.</p><p>“And that's what they try to make you do,” Johnson said. “And you combine that with the fact that it's hard for a lot of offenses to even get started. …. It's hard to run the ball, hard to throw the ball, and it's going to take a team effort to win this one here this week. </p><p>It will take an outstanding effort from the quarterback, too.</p><p>The most famous one in the world just learned that the hard way.</p><p>“They’re fully equipped over there to do whatever they need as a defense and as a team …” Williams said. “It’s going to be a fun challenge for us.”</p>

entries.summary: <p>Met with cheers, T-shirts and voter guides, hundreds of Chicago high school students flooded the Loop early voting supersite Wednesday as part of a push for young voter participation.</p><p>Chicago Votes, a political organization with a focus on young people, sponsored the Parade to the Polls, busing students from school to the Loop site so they could cast their ballots in the upcoming general election, many of them for the first time. entries.title: Bears QB Caleb Williams to keep wearing Caddix cleats, even with NFL fines looming
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/10/25/bears-qb-caleb-williams-fined-11-941-for-wearing-tom-brady-backed-caddix-cleats-another-fine-likely-coming" target="_blank" >Bears</a> quarterback Caleb Williams will continue wearing what he calls his “science cleats,” even if the NFL keeps fining him.</p><p>Williams was fined $11,941 <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/10/25/bears-qb-caleb-williams-fined-11-941-for-wearing-tom-brady-backed-caddix-cleats-another-fine-likely-coming" target="_blank" >for wearing Caddix cleats</a> against the Falcons. The NFL allows only Nike, Adidas and Under Armour shoes to display their logos on game day. Williams wore black cleats with a prominent Caddix logo against the Falcons and did so again Thursday against the Patriots. He’s yet to be fined from the Patriots game, but it’s likely on the way.</p><p>“I’m focused on being able to be out here for the guys,” Williams said Wednesday. “And if that can give me a small percentage up [as a fine] and it works, then that’s what I’m gonna do.”</p><p>Caddix claims its “smartstuds” flex and release when players move, reducing stress on joints. About 40 players wear them — as does former star Tom Brady.<br>Williams wore all-white Caddix cleats earlier in the season and was not fined. Asked whether they prevented his hamstring injury from being any worse when he wore them against the Vikings, Williams demurred.</p><p>“If I had that answer, I’d be a trillionaire and sitting somewhere nice …” he said with a smile. “I think my joints, my ankles and my knees and my feet haven’t bothered me as much from the other cleats that I’ve worn. … They’ve worked for me, and I feel that I feel a difference. That’s my opinion, and somebody else can have another.”</p><p>Caddix CEO Jack Rasmussen said in a statement that the company will pay any fine for him.</p>
entries.author: Patrick Finley
